people.name: Polycarp of Smyrna
people.summary: Bishop of Smyrna, linked by Irenaeus to the apostle John; martyred in old age around 155–156.

people.name: Melito of Sardis
people.summary: Bishop of Sardis (d. c. 180) whose Easter sermon On Pascha reads the Exodus as a picture of Christ.

people.name: Hippolytus of Rome
people.summary: Roman presbyter and writer against heresies; died in exile in Sardinia around 235.

people.name: Cyprian of Carthage
people.summary: Bishop of Carthage during the Decian persecution; wrote on the unity of the church; martyred in 258.

people.name: Ephrem the Syrian
people.summary: Deacon of Nisibis and Edessa whose Syriac hymns teach theology through poetry and imagery.

people.name: Cyril of Jerusalem
people.summary: Bishop of Jerusalem whose Catechetical Lectures show how new believers were taught in the fourth century.

people.name: Ambrose of Milan
people.summary: Bishop of Milan, hymn writer and preacher, who baptised Augustine in 387.

people.name: Pelagius
people.summary: British-born ascetic teacher in Rome (c. 354–c. 418) whose stress on human freedom provoked Augustine's doctrine of grace.

people.name: Arius
people.summary: Alexandrian presbyter who taught that the Son was a created being; his teaching was rejected at Nicaea in 325.

people.name: Nestorius
people.summary: Archbishop of Constantinople (428–431), deposed at Ephesus in 431 over how Christ's two natures are united.

people.name: Leo the Great
people.summary: Bishop of Rome (440–461) whose Tome on Christ's two natures was received at Chalcedon in 451.

people.name: Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite
people.summary: Anonymous Syrian writer (c. 500) who wrote under the name of Paul's convert in Acts 17:34; shaped mystical theology East and West.

people.name: Benedict of Nursia
people.summary: Founder of Monte Cassino whose Rule became the pattern for Western monastic life.

people.name: Gregory the Great
people.summary: Bishop of Rome (590–604), pastoral writer and organiser of the mission to the English.

people.name: Symeon the New Theologian
people.summary: Byzantine monk and abbot who taught that believers can consciously experience the light and life of God.

people.name: Peter Abelard
people.summary: Paris teacher who stressed the cross as the supreme display of God's love that kindles love in us.

people.name: Peter Lombard
people.summary: Bishop of Paris whose Four Books of Sentences became the standard theology textbook of the medieval schools.

people.name: Francis of Assisi
people.summary: Italian friar who embraced poverty, preached peace and founded the Franciscan order.

people.name: Gregory Palamas
people.summary: Athonite monk and archbishop of Thessalonica who defended hesychast prayer and the essence–energies distinction.

people.name: Julian of Norwich
people.summary: English anchoress whose Revelations of Divine Love is the earliest surviving book in English by a woman.

people.name: John Wycliffe
people.summary: Oxford theologian who challenged papal authority and inspired the first complete English Bible.

people.name: Jan Hus
people.summary: Prague preacher and reformer burned at the Council of Constance in 1415.

people.name: Huldrych Zwingli
people.summary: Reformer of Zürich who began expository preaching through Matthew in 1519; killed at Kappel in 1531.

people.name: Thomas Cranmer
people.summary: Archbishop of Canterbury and author of the Book of Common Prayer; burned under Mary I.

people.name: Philip Melanchthon
people.summary: Luther's colleague at Wittenberg and principal author of the Augsburg Confession.

people.name: Conrad Grebel
people.summary: Zürich leader who performed the first adult re-baptisms in January 1525.

people.name: Michael Sattler
people.summary: Former monk and Anabaptist leader associated with the Schleitheim Confession; executed in 1527.

people.name: Menno Simons
people.summary: Dutch priest turned Anabaptist leader whose writings gave the Mennonites their name.

people.name: Ignatius of Loyola
people.summary: Basque founder of the Society of Jesus (Jesuits) and author of the Spiritual Exercises.

people.name: John Knox
people.summary: Leader of the Scottish Reformation and shaper of Presbyterian church order.

people.name: Theodore Beza
people.summary: Calvin's successor at Geneva who systematised Reformed teaching on predestination.

people.name: Jacobus Arminius
people.summary: Leiden professor who questioned unconditional predestination; his followers issued the Remonstrance of 1610.

people.name: John Smyth
people.summary: English Separatist who led the first English Baptist congregation in Amsterdam in 1609.

people.name: John Owen
people.summary: English Puritan theologian whose Death of Death (1647) defended definite atonement.

people.name: George Fox
people.summary: Founder of the Religious Society of Friends, who taught the Inward Light of Christ.

people.name: Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf
people.summary: Saxon count who sheltered Moravian refugees at Herrnhut and launched their worldwide mission.

people.name: John Wesley
people.summary: Anglican priest whose field preaching and societies began Methodism; taught assurance and Christian perfection.

people.name: Charles Wesley
people.summary: Anglican priest and co-founder of Methodism who wrote thousands of hymns.

people.name: George Whitefield
people.summary: Calvinistic Methodist evangelist whose open-air preaching spread the Great Awakening on both sides of the Atlantic.

people.name: William Carey
people.summary: English Baptist missionary to India and Bible translator; often called the father of modern missions.

people.name: Barton W. Stone
people.summary: Presbyterian minister at the Cane Ridge revival (1801) who later joined the Restoration Movement.

people.name: William Miller
people.summary: Baptist lay preacher who predicted Christ's return around 1843–1844.

people.name: Alexander Campbell
people.summary: Leader of the Restoration Movement seeking to restore New Testament Christianity without creeds.

people.name: Charles G. Finney
people.summary: American revivalist and Oberlin professor who promoted 'new measures' in revival.

people.name: John Nelson Darby
people.summary: Anglo-Irish former Anglican clergyman, leader among the Plymouth Brethren and chief architect of dispensationalism.

people.name: Phoebe Palmer
people.summary: Methodist lay teacher whose 'altar theology' shaped the Holiness movement.

people.name: Ellen G. White
people.summary: Co-founder of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, regarded by Adventists as having a prophetic gift.

people.name: J. Hudson Taylor
people.summary: English missionary who founded the China Inland Mission in 1865.

people.name: Charles H. Spurgeon
people.summary: London Baptist preacher at the Metropolitan Tabernacle; the most widely read preacher of his century.

people.name: Dwight L. Moody
people.summary: American evangelist and founder of what became the Moody Bible Institute.

people.name: Joseph Rabinowitz
people.summary: Jewish leader in Kishinev who founded a congregation of 'Israelites of the New Covenant' in the 1880s.

people.name: C. I. Scofield
people.summary: American Bible teacher whose Scofield Reference Bible (1909) popularised dispensationalism.

people.name: William J. Seymour
people.summary: African American Holiness preacher who led the Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles from 1906.

people.name: Charles F. Parham
people.summary: Kansas Bible-school leader who taught tongues as the evidence of Spirit baptism (1901).

people.name: Karl Barth
people.summary: Swiss Reformed theologian whose Church Dogmatics re-centred theology on God's self-revelation in Jesus Christ.

people.name: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
people.summary: German Lutheran pastor of the Confessing Church, executed by the Nazi regime in 1945.

people.name: Billy Graham
people.summary: American evangelist whose crusades from 1949 shaped post-war evangelicalism.

entries.title: Pentecost: the Spirit poured out
entries.summary: Fifty days after the resurrection the Spirit comes on the disciples in Jerusalem, and Peter's sermon gathers about three thousand. The date is c. 30 or 33, depending on the year of the crucifixion.

entries.title: Stephen, the first martyr
entries.summary: Stephen, one of the Seven, is stoned after his speech to the Sanhedrin; the persecution that follows scatters believers through Judea and Samaria. Dates around 33–36.

entries.title: Saul meets the risen Jesus
entries.summary: On the road to Damascus the persecutor Saul encounters the risen Christ and is called to take the good news to the nations. Usually dated 33–36.

entries.title: Gentiles receive the Spirit
entries.summary: Peter preaches in the house of the Roman centurion Cornelius at Caesarea, the Spirit falls on Gentiles, and they are baptised without becoming Jews.

entries.title: Disciples first called 'Christians' at Antioch
entries.summary: A mixed Jewish and Gentile church grows in Antioch, Syria's capital, where Barnabas and Saul teach for a year and the disciples are first called Christians.

entries.title: James son of Zebedee executed
entries.summary: Herod Agrippa I beheads James the brother of John and imprisons Peter, shortly before Herod's own death in 44.

entries.title: Paul's missionary journeys
entries.summary: From Antioch, Paul and his companions plant churches across Cyprus, Galatia, Macedonia, Achaia and Asia, usually starting in the synagogue.

entries.title: Paul's letters written
entries.summary: Paul writes to the churches he founded and to Rome. Galatians and 1 Thessalonians are among the earliest; the dates of the Pastoral Epistles are debated.

entries.title: Council of Jerusalem
entries.summary: Apostles and elders decide that Gentile believers need not be circumcised or keep the whole Law of Moses, asking only a few things for table fellowship. Usually dated 48–50.

entries.title: Claudius expels Jews from Rome
entries.summary: The emperor Claudius expels Jews from Rome after disturbances (Suetonius mentions 'Chrestus'); Priscilla and Aquila move to Corinth.

entries.title: Nero's persecution in Rome
entries.summary: After the great fire of Rome in July 64, Nero blames the Christians and has many put to death, as Tacitus reports (Annals 15.44).

entries.title: Peter and Paul martyred in Rome
entries.summary: Early tradition (1 Clement 5, Eusebius) places the deaths of Peter and Paul in Rome under Nero. Exact years are uncertain.

entries.title: The Gospels written
entries.summary: Mark, Matthew, Luke and John are written, by most estimates between the 60s and 90s. A minority dates all four before 70.

entries.title: The Jewish revolt against Rome
entries.summary: Judea revolts against Rome; the war ends with the fall of Masada in 73 or 74. Eusebius reports that Jerusalem's Christians fled to Pella beforehand.

entries.title: Jerusalem and the Temple destroyed
entries.summary: Titus captures Jerusalem and burns the Temple in August 70, within a generation of Jesus' warning. Partial-preterist readers see much of Matt 24 fulfilled here.

entries.title: 1 Clement sent from Rome to Corinth
entries.summary: The Roman church writes to Corinth urging reconciliation after the removal of elders: one of the earliest Christian writings outside the New Testament. Some date it earlier.

entries.title: Ignatius writes on the way to martyrdom
entries.summary: Under guard on the way to Rome, Bishop Ignatius of Antioch writes seven letters on union with Christ, the Eucharist and church unity. Usually dated c. 107–115.

entries.title: Pliny writes to Trajan about Christians
entries.summary: Pliny, governor of Bithynia, describes Christians singing a hymn to Christ 'as to a god' and asks how to treat them; Trajan replies that they are not to be sought out.

entries.title: Marcion excommunicated in Rome
entries.summary: Marcion rejects the Old Testament God and publishes an edited canon of Luke and ten Pauline letters; the church's response sharpens questions of canon.

entries.title: Martyrdom of Polycarp
entries.summary: Polycarp, aged bishop of Smyrna, is burned in the stadium; the account of his death is the earliest martyr narrative outside the New Testament. Dated c. 155–156 (some say later).

entries.title: Justin and companions martyred
entries.summary: The philosopher-apologist Justin is beheaded in Rome with six companions under the prefect Rusticus.

entries.title: Martyrs of Lyons and Vienne
entries.summary: Mob violence and trials in Gaul kill many Christians, including the slave girl Blandina; Eusebius preserves the churches' letter describing it.

entries.title: Irenaeus writes Against Heresies
entries.summary: Irenaeus of Lyons answers the Gnostics with the rule of faith, the fourfold Gospel and his theology of recapitulation.

entries.title: The Quartodeciman (Easter date) controversy
entries.summary: Victor of Rome tries to excommunicate the churches of Asia for keeping Pascha on 14 Nisan; Irenaeus urges peace.

entries.title: Tertullian coins 'Trinity' in Latin
entries.summary: In Against Praxeas Tertullian uses *trinitas* and speaks of one substance in three persons.

entries.title: Origen's On First Principles
entries.summary: Origen writes the first systematic theology, on God, creation, freedom and the final restoration. Dated c. 220–230.

entries.title: Decian persecution
entries.summary: Emperor Decius requires all citizens to sacrifice and obtain a certificate; many Christians lapse, raising the question of how to restore them.

entries.title: Cyprian martyred at Carthage
entries.summary: Under Valerian's persecution Bishop Cyprian is beheaded; Sixtus II of Rome and his deacon Lawrence also die.

entries.title: Antony goes into the desert
entries.summary: Antony of Egypt hears Matt 19:21 read in church, sells his goods and withdraws to the desert, beginning the monastic movement. Dated c. 270.

entries.title: Armenia becomes Christian
entries.summary: King Tiridates III is baptised by Gregory the Illuminator and Armenia becomes the first kingdom to adopt Christianity. The traditional date is 301; some scholars prefer c. 314.

entries.title: The Great Persecution
entries.summary: Diocletian and Galerius order churches destroyed, Scriptures burned and clergy arrested; the persecution ends in the West sooner than in the East.

entries.title: Donatist schism in North Africa
entries.summary: A dispute over clergy who handed over Scriptures in persecution divides the African church for a century; Augustine argues against the Donatists.

entries.title: Constantine turns to Christ
entries.summary: Before the battle of the Milvian Bridge Constantine adopts the Chi-Rho sign. His favour changes the church's place in the empire.

entries.title: Edict of Milan
entries.summary: Constantine and Licinius grant freedom of worship and order the return of confiscated church property, ending persecution in most of the empire.

entries.title: Council of Nicaea
entries.summary: The first ecumenical council rejects Arius' teaching that the Son is a creature, confesses the Son 'of one being' (*homoousios*) with the Father, and settles a common date for Easter.

entries.title: The Gospel in Aksum (Ethiopia)
entries.summary: Frumentius, consecrated bishop by Athanasius, evangelises the kingdom of Aksum, whose King Ezana adopts Christianity in the mid-fourth century.

entries.title: Ulfilas and the Gothic Bible
entries.summary: Ulfilas is consecrated bishop for the Goths, invents a Gothic alphabet and translates the Bible. His Christianity is Homoian (non-Nicene).

entries.title: Athanasius lists the 27 New Testament books
entries.summary: Athanasius' Festal Letter 39 is the earliest list of exactly the 27 books of the New Testament.

entries.title: The Cappadocian Fathers
entries.summary: Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus and Gregory of Nyssa articulate one being in three persons and defend the Spirit's deity.

entries.title: First Council of Constantinople
entries.summary: The second ecumenical council confirms Nicaea, affirms the Holy Spirit as 'Lord and giver of life' worshipped with the Father and Son, and rejects Apollinarius.

entries.title: Jerome's Vulgate
entries.summary: Commissioned by Pope Damasus, Jerome revises the Latin Gospels and later translates most of the Old Testament from Hebrew. It becomes the Western church's Bible.

entries.title: Augustine converted and baptised
entries.summary: In a Milan garden Augustine reads Rom 13:13–14 and is converted; Ambrose baptises him at Easter 387.

entries.title: Councils of Hippo and Carthage list the canon
entries.summary: North African councils list the books of Scripture, including the Old Testament books later called deuterocanonical.

entries.title: Synod of Seleucia-Ctesiphon
entries.summary: The church in the Persian Empire organises under the bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon and adopts the Nicene Creed: a milestone of the Church of the East.

entries.title: The Pelagian controversy
entries.summary: Augustine opposes Pelagius and Caelestius on grace, the fall and infant baptism; the Council of Carthage (418) condemns Pelagian teaching.

entries.title: Augustine writes The City of God
entries.summary: After the sack of Rome (410) Augustine answers pagan critics and contrasts the earthly and heavenly cities.

entries.title: Council of Ephesus
entries.summary: The third ecumenical council, led by Cyril of Alexandria, deposes Nestorius and affirms Mary as *Theotokos*: the one born of her is God the Word incarnate.

entries.title: Patrick's mission to Ireland
entries.summary: Patrick, a Briton once enslaved in Ireland, returns as a missionary bishop. The traditional date is 432.

entries.title: Council of Chalcedon
entries.summary: The fourth ecumenical council confesses one Christ 'in two natures', without confusion, change, division or separation, drawing on Leo's Tome.

entries.title: Oriental Orthodox churches part ways
entries.summary: Churches in Egypt, Syria, Armenia and Ethiopia reject Chalcedon's 'two natures' formula, keeping Cyril's 'one incarnate nature of God the Word'.

entries.title: Benedict founds Monte Cassino
entries.summary: Benedict establishes his monastery and writes the Rule that will shape Western monastic life.

entries.title: Council of Orange
entries.summary: A regional council in Gaul affirms Augustine's teaching that grace precedes and enables faith, without endorsing predestination to evil.

entries.title: Second Council of Constantinople
entries.summary: The fifth ecumenical council condemns the 'Three Chapters' to reconcile the non-Chalcedonians. Anathemas against Origenist teaching are linked with this period.

entries.title: Third Council of Toledo and the filioque
entries.summary: As the Visigoths renounce Arianism, the creed is recited in Spain with 'and the Son' (*filioque*) added to the Spirit's procession.

entries.title: Gregory sends Augustine to England
entries.summary: Pope Gregory the Great sends the monk Augustine to Kent, where King Æthelberht is baptised.

entries.title: Church of the East reaches China
entries.summary: The Persian monk Alopen arrives at the Tang capital Chang'an; the Xi'an Stele (781) records the mission.

entries.title: Third Council of Constantinople
entries.summary: The sixth ecumenical council affirms that Christ has two wills, divine and human, vindicating Maximus the Confessor.

entries.title: Boniface's mission to the Germans
entries.summary: The English monk Boniface evangelises and organises the church in Germany; he is killed in Frisia in 754.

entries.title: Iconoclast controversy
entries.summary: Byzantine emperors ban icons; defenders such as John of Damascus argue that the incarnation makes images of Christ possible. Icons are restored in 843.

entries.title: Second Council of Nicaea
entries.summary: The seventh ecumenical council approves the veneration (not worship) of icons, because honour given to the image passes to its prototype.

entries.title: Cyril and Methodius to the Slavs
entries.summary: The brothers from Thessalonica go to Moravia, create the Glagolitic alphabet and translate Scripture and liturgy into Slavonic.

entries.title: The Photian schism
entries.summary: Rome and Constantinople clash over Patriarch Photius, the mission to Bulgaria and the filioque; communion is later restored.

entries.title: Baptism of Kievan Rus'
entries.summary: Prince Vladimir of Kiev is baptised and his people follow, bringing Byzantine Christianity to the Eastern Slavs.

entries.title: The Great Schism
entries.summary: Papal legates and Patriarch Michael Cerularius excommunicate each other in Constantinople. The break deepens over the following centuries; the excommunications were lifted in 1965.

entries.title: First Crusade and the Rhineland massacres
entries.summary: Responding to Urban II's call (1095), crusading bands massacre Jewish communities in the Rhineland before taking Jerusalem in 1099.

entries.title: Anselm's Cur Deus Homo
entries.summary: Anselm explains the incarnation and atonement as satisfaction for the honour of God, setting the agenda for Western atonement theology. Completed 1098.

entries.title: Peter Lombard's Sentences
entries.summary: Lombard's Four Books of Sentences becomes the standard textbook of medieval theology. Dated c. 1150–1158.

entries.title: Crusaders sack Constantinople
entries.summary: The Fourth Crusade loots Constantinople and sets up a Latin empire, hardening Orthodox estrangement from Rome.

entries.title: Francis and the Friars Minor
entries.summary: Innocent III approves Francis' simple rule of gospel poverty for his brotherhood.

entries.title: Fourth Lateran Council
entries.summary: The council uses the term 'transubstantiation', requires annual confession and communion, and imposes distinctive dress on Jews.

entries.title: Aquinas writes the Summa Theologiae
entries.summary: Thomas Aquinas' unfinished Summa integrates Aristotle and Christian doctrine; it includes Anselm's satisfaction theory.

entries.title: Second Council of Lyon
entries.summary: A short-lived reunion with the Byzantines; the profession of faith presented at the council includes the filioque and purgatory.

entries.title: Councils uphold Palamas
entries.summary: Councils in Constantinople affirm Gregory Palamas' teaching on the uncreated light and the essence–energies distinction.

entries.title: Julian of Norwich's showings
entries.summary: During severe illness Julian receives sixteen visions of Christ's love, later written as Revelations of Divine Love.

entries.title: The Western (Papal) Schism
entries.summary: Two, then three, rival popes divide Latin Christendom until the Council of Constance restores a single papacy.

entries.title: The Wycliffe Bible
entries.summary: Followers of John Wycliffe translate the whole Bible from the Latin Vulgate into English; it circulates in manuscript.

entries.title: Jan Hus burned at Constance
entries.summary: Despite a safe-conduct, the Council of Constance condemns and burns the Bohemian reformer Jan Hus.

entries.title: Council of Florence
entries.summary: Byzantine and Latin delegates agree a union (including the filioque and purgatory) that is rejected in the East, notably by Mark of Ephesus.

entries.title: Gutenberg prints the Bible
entries.summary: The Latin Bible printed with movable type in Mainz (c. 1454–1455) opens the age of print.

entries.title: Erasmus' Greek New Testament
entries.summary: Erasmus publishes the Greek New Testament with a fresh Latin translation; it becomes the basis of Reformation translations.

entries.title: Luther's Ninety-five Theses
entries.summary: On 31 October 1517 Martin Luther sends his theses against the sale of indulgences, sparking the Reformation.

entries.title: Luther at the Diet of Worms
entries.summary: Luther refuses to recant unless convinced by Scripture and plain reason; he is declared an outlaw and hidden at the Wartburg, where he translates the New Testament.

entries.title: Zwingli's Reformation in Zürich
entries.summary: After a public disputation the Zürich council adopts Zwingli's Sixty-seven Articles.

entries.title: First Anabaptist baptisms
entries.summary: On 21 January 1525 Conrad Grebel baptises George Blaurock in Zürich, beginning the Anabaptist movement.

entries.title: Tyndale's English New Testament
entries.summary: William Tyndale's New Testament, translated from Greek, is printed at Worms and smuggled into England.

entries.title: Schleitheim Confession
entries.summary: Swiss Brethren agree seven articles on believer's baptism, separation from the world and refusal of the sword and oath.

entries.title: Augsburg Confession
entries.summary: Melanchthon's statement of Lutheran faith is presented to Emperor Charles V; it remains the chief Lutheran confession.

entries.title: Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy
entries.summary: Parliament declares the king Supreme Head of the Church of England, breaking with Rome.

entries.title: Calvin's Institutes first published
entries.summary: John Calvin publishes the first edition of the Institutes of the Christian Religion in Basel; the final edition appears in 1559.

entries.title: Menno Simons joins the Anabaptists
entries.summary: Menno leaves the priesthood and gathers scattered peaceful Anabaptists in the Netherlands and North Germany.

entries.title: Jesuits founded; Xavier to Asia
entries.summary: Paul III approves the Society of Jesus; Francis Xavier sails for India in 1541 and reaches Japan in 1549.

entries.title: Council of Trent
entries.summary: Rome's response to the Reformation defines Scripture and tradition, justification, the seven sacraments and purgatory, and launches reform.

entries.title: First Book of Common Prayer
entries.summary: Thomas Cranmer's English liturgy replaces the Latin services in the Church of England.

entries.title: Peace of Augsburg
entries.summary: The empire allows each prince to choose Lutheranism or Catholicism for his territory.

entries.title: Scottish Reformation
entries.summary: Parliament adopts the Scots Confession prepared by John Knox and colleagues.

entries.title: Thirty-Nine Articles
entries.summary: The Church of England's doctrinal articles receive final parliamentary approval.

entries.title: St Bartholomew's Day massacre
entries.summary: Thousands of French Huguenots (Protestants) are killed in Paris and other cities.

entries.title: First English Baptist congregation
entries.summary: John Smyth and Thomas Helwys's congregation of English exiles in Amsterdam practise believer's baptism.

entries.title: The Remonstrance
entries.summary: Followers of Arminius present five articles against unconditional election and limited atonement.

entries.title: The King James Version
entries.summary: The Authorised Version, commissioned by James I in 1604, is published; it becomes the dominant English Bible for three centuries.

entries.title: Synod of Dort
entries.summary: The Dutch Reformed synod rejects the Remonstrants and issues the Canons of Dort, the source of the later 'five points of Calvinism'.

entries.title: Westminster Confession of Faith
entries.summary: The Westminster Assembly (1643–1653) produces the Confession and Catechisms, the standards of Presbyterianism.

entries.title: George Fox and the Quakers
entries.summary: After his vision on Pendle Hill, Fox gathers the Society of Friends, teaching the Inward Light of Christ.

entries.title: Spener's Pia Desideria and Pietism
entries.summary: Philipp Jakob Spener calls Lutherans to heartfelt faith, Bible study groups and holy living.

entries.title: Moravian revival at Herrnhut
entries.summary: On 13 August 1727 the refugee community on Zinzendorf's estate experiences a renewal; a hundred-year prayer watch and missions follow.

entries.title: Moravian missionaries sail
entries.summary: The first Moravian missionaries leave for the Danish West Indies, beginning Protestant cross-cultural missions on a large scale.

entries.title: The First Great Awakening
entries.summary: Revival under Jonathan Edwards in Northampton and George Whitefield's preaching tours sweeps the American colonies.

entries.title: Wesley's heart 'strangely warmed'
entries.summary: On 24 May 1738 John Wesley finds assurance of faith while hearing Luther's preface to Romans read; Methodism follows.

entries.title: 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God'
entries.summary: Jonathan Edwards preaches his famous sermon at Enfield, Connecticut; it becomes the emblem of hellfire preaching.

entries.title: The Second Great Awakening
entries.summary: Revivals in America's frontier and northeast, including camp meetings and Finney's campaigns, reshape American Protestantism.

entries.title: William Carey sails for India
entries.summary: After his Enquiry (1792) and the founding of the Baptist Missionary Society, Carey goes to Bengal.

entries.title: Cane Ridge camp meeting
entries.summary: Thousands gather in Kentucky for a week-long communion and camp meeting led by Barton Stone and others.

entries.title: The Restoration Movement
entries.summary: Thomas Campbell's Declaration and Address calls for unity on the Bible alone; with Alexander Campbell and Barton Stone it forms the Churches of Christ and Disciples.

entries.title: Powerscourt conferences and Darby
entries.summary: Prophecy conferences in Ireland help John Nelson Darby develop a secret pre-tribulation rapture and the Israel–church distinction.

entries.title: The Great Disappointment
entries.summary: William Miller's followers expect Christ on 22 October 1844; out of the disappointment the Seventh-day Adventist Church later emerges.

entries.title: China Inland Mission founded
entries.summary: Hudson Taylor founds a mission whose workers dress in Chinese style and go into the interior.

entries.title: First Vatican Council
entries.summary: Defines papal infallibility when the pope speaks *ex cathedra* on faith and morals.

entries.title: Keswick Convention begins
entries.summary: An annual gathering in England's Lake District promoting 'the higher Christian life'.

entries.title: Niagara Bible Conference
entries.summary: Annual conferences spread premillennial and dispensational teaching among American evangelicals.

entries.title: Tongues at Topeka
entries.summary: At Charles Parham's Bible school in Kansas, Agnes Ozman speaks in tongues on 1 January 1901; Parham teaches tongues as evidence of Spirit baptism.

entries.title: The Welsh Revival
entries.summary: Revival under Evan Roberts and others spreads across Wales.

entries.title: Azusa Street Revival
entries.summary: William J. Seymour leads an interracial revival in Los Angeles that launches worldwide Pentecostalism.

entries.title: The Great Pyongyang Revival
entries.summary: Confession and prayer revival among Korean Presbyterians, a landmark for Korean Christianity.

entries.title: The Scofield Reference Bible
entries.summary: Oxford University Press publishes C. I. Scofield's annotated KJV, whose notes spread dispensationalism.

entries.title: Edinburgh World Missionary Conference
entries.summary: A landmark missions conference that also gives birth to the modern ecumenical movement.

entries.title: The Fundamentals published
entries.summary: Ninety essays defending core doctrines against liberal theology give 'fundamentalism' its name.

entries.title: Assemblies of God organised
entries.summary: Pentecostal ministers meet in Hot Springs, Arkansas, to form what becomes the largest Pentecostal denomination.

entries.title: Barth's Epistle to the Romans
entries.summary: Karl Barth's commentary breaks with liberal Protestantism and starts 'dialectical theology'. A revised edition appears in 1922.

entries.title: Aulén's Christus Victor
entries.summary: Gustaf Aulén argues that the 'classic' patristic view of atonement is God's victory over the powers. English translation 1931.

entries.title: Barmen Declaration
entries.summary: The Confessing Church rejects Nazi control of the German church, confessing Jesus Christ as the one Word of God.

entries.title: The Holocaust
entries.summary: Six million Jews are murdered by Nazi Germany. Its shadow forces churches to confront Christian anti-Judaism.

entries.title: Bonhoeffer executed
entries.summary: Dietrich Bonhoeffer is hanged at Flossenbürg in April 1945, weeks before the war ends.

entries.title: Dead Sea Scrolls discovered
entries.summary: Scrolls found near Qumran include the oldest known manuscripts of the Hebrew Bible and illuminate Second Temple Judaism.

entries.title: World Council of Churches founded
entries.summary: Protestant and Orthodox churches form the World Council of Churches in Amsterdam.

entries.title: Billy Graham's Los Angeles crusade
entries.summary: An eight-week tent campaign makes Billy Graham a national figure and shapes post-war evangelicalism.

entries.title: Charismatic renewal in mainline churches
entries.summary: Episcopal priest Dennis Bennett's announcement in Van Nuys, California, marks the spread of Spirit baptism into historic denominations.

entries.title: Second Vatican Council
entries.summary: Reforms Catholic worship (vernacular liturgy), opens dialogue with other Christians and religions, and repudiates blaming Jews collectively for Christ's death (Nostra Aetate).

entries.title: Rome and Constantinople lift the 1054 excommunications
entries.summary: Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras I jointly regret and remove the mutual excommunications of 1054.

entries.title: Catholic Charismatic Renewal
entries.summary: A retreat at Duquesne University begins charismatic renewal among Roman Catholics.

entries.title: The Jesus Movement
entries.summary: Hippies and young people come to faith in California and beyond, influencing contemporary worship music.

entries.title: The Late Great Planet Earth
entries.summary: Hal Lindsey's bestseller popularises dispensational end-times prophecy.

entries.title: Lausanne Congress on World Evangelization
entries.summary: Evangelicals from 150 countries adopt the Lausanne Covenant, joining evangelism and social responsibility.

entries.title: Messianic Jewish Alliance of America
entries.summary: The Hebrew Christian Alliance of America renames itself, signalling a movement of Jewish believers keeping Jewish identity.

entries.title: The 'New Perspective' on Paul
entries.summary: E. P. Sanders' Paul and Palestinian Judaism challenges the picture of first-century Judaism as legalistic; Dunn and Wright develop the 'new perspective'.

entries.title: Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification
entries.summary: The Lutheran World Federation and the Roman Catholic Church declare a consensus on basic truths of justification.

entries.title: Christianity's centre shifts south
entries.summary: By the early twenty-first century most Christians live in Africa, Latin America and Asia; Pentecostal and charismatic forms grow fastest.

entries.title: Eastern Orthodox Church
entries.subtitle: Orthodox
entries.summary: A communion of self-governing churches (Constantinople, Antioch, Jerusalem, Russia, Greece, Romania and others) that see themselves as the continuation of the undivided early church.

distinctives: Theosis (deification) as the goal of salvation

entries.title: Oriental Orthodox Churches
entries.subtitle: Orthodox (non-Chalcedonian)
entries.summary: The Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian, Eritrean and Malankara churches, which did not accept the Council of Chalcedon (451).

distinctives: Accept the first three ecumenical councils
Miaphysite Christology: one incarnate nature of God the Word
Ancient liturgies in Coptic, Syriac, Armenian and Ge'ez

entries.title: Assyrian Church of the East
entries.subtitle: Church of the East
entries.summary: The ancient church of the Persian Empire, which spread along the Silk Road to India, Central Asia and China.

distinctives: Honours Theodore of Mopsuestia and Nestorius' teachers
Historic missionary reach across Asia to China

entries.title: Roman Catholic Church
entries.subtitle: Catholic
entries.summary: The largest Christian body, about 1.3 billion members, in communion with the pope as bishop of Rome.

founders: The apostles, with Peter as first bishop of Rome (Catholic teaching)
distinctives: Communion with the bishop of Rome
Scripture and Tradition with the Magisterium

entries.title: Eastern Catholic Churches
entries.subtitle: Catholic
entries.summary: Churches with Byzantine, Syriac, Armenian, Coptic and other Eastern traditions in communion with Rome.

founders: Various unions with Rome (e.g. Union of Brest 1596)
distinctives: Own canon law (1990 Code for Eastern churches)

entries.title: Lutheran Churches
entries.subtitle: Protestant (Lutheran)
entries.summary: Churches shaped by Martin Luther's Reformation and the Augsburg Confession.

distinctives: Real presence of Christ in the Supper

entries.title: Reformed and Presbyterian Churches
entries.subtitle: Protestant (Reformed)
entries.summary: Churches from the Swiss Reformation of Zwingli and Calvin, including Presbyterians and continental Reformed.

distinctives: Westminster Standards or Three Forms of Unity

entries.title: Anglican Communion
entries.subtitle: Protestant/Catholic (Anglican)
entries.summary: The Church of England and related provinces worldwide, about 85 million members.

entries.title: Anabaptists and Mennonites
entries.subtitle: Anabaptist

entries.title: Baptists
entries.subtitle: Protestant (Free Church)
entries.summary: Churches practising believer's baptism and local church autonomy, from English Separatism.

entries.title: Methodists
entries.subtitle: Protestant (Wesleyan)
entries.summary: Churches from the Wesleys' revival within the Church of England.

entries.title: Congregationalists

entries.title: Pentecostals

entries.title: Charismatic Movement

entries.title: Seventh-day Adventists
entries.subtitle: Adventist

blocks.subject: person:irenaeus
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Irenaeus grew up in Smyrna in Asia Minor, where as a young man he heard Polycarp, who had known the apostle John. He moved to Gaul and became bishop of Lyons after the persecution of 177. His great work, *Against Heresies* (c. 180), answers the Valentinian Gnostics; his shorter *Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching* summarises the faith for a friend. He is the first great theologian of the whole biblical story, from Adam to the new creation.

blocks.subject: person:irenaeus
blocks.title: Atonement as recapitulation
blocks.body:
Irenaeus pictures the Son "summing up" (*anakephalaiōsis*, Eph 1:10) the whole human story in himself. Where Adam failed, Christ retraced the path and obeyed: disobedience at a tree is undone by obedience on a tree, and the virgin Eve's unbelief by the virgin Mary's faith. Salvation is humanity healed and restored in the person of the Son, not a payment made to the Father.

He also speaks of Christ redeeming us "by his own blood" from the apostasy that had enslaved us, yet insists that God did this justly and by persuasion, not by seizing what was the devil's by force.

blocks.subject: person:irenaeus
blocks.title: Union and sonship
blocks.body:
For Irenaeus the goal of the incarnation is that we share in God's life. The Word became what we are so that he might bring us to be what he is; the Son of God became a son of man so that we might receive adoption and become sons of God. The glory of God is a human being fully alive, and that life consists in seeing God.

He reads Adam and Eve as children who were meant to grow into maturity, so the story is one of growth toward communion, interrupted by the fall and completed in Christ.

blocks.subject: person:irenaeus
blocks.title: Trinity: the Father's two hands
blocks.body: Irenaeus describes the Son and the Spirit as the Father's "two hands" by which he made humanity and through which he still shapes it. The Father needed no angels to create: the Word and Wisdom were always with him. This is an early, relational picture of the one God acting as Father, Son and Spirit.

blocks.subject: person:irenaeus
blocks.title: Kingdom and the renewed earth
blocks.body: Irenaeus expected the righteous to reign with Christ in a renewed creation, where the promise of land to Abraham is fulfilled literally before the final vision of God. He was a millennialist (chiliast), and the app's postmillennial reading differs from him here; what it shares is his conviction that God's purpose is the healing of this world, not escape from it.

blocks.subject: person:athanasius
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Athanasius was bishop of Alexandria from 328 to 373. As a young deacon he attended the Council of Nicaea (325) and spent the rest of his life defending its teaching that the Son is fully God. He was exiled five times. His *On the Incarnation* explains why the Word became flesh; his *Festal Letter 39* (367) is the first list of exactly the 27 New Testament books.

blocks.subject: person:athanasius
blocks.title: Atonement: rescuing a dying creation
blocks.body:
In *On the Incarnation* the problem is not first an offended God but a creation sliding back into corruption and non-being after turning from the Word. Repentance alone could not reverse corruption that had taken hold of human nature. So the Word took a body, offered it to death on behalf of all, and by the resurrection abolished death and clothed the mortal with immortality.

Athanasius does use the language of a debt owed and of death "in the place of all", but the frame is the healing of nature and the defeat of death, which is why later writers read him as a key witness to Christus Victor.

blocks.subject: person:athanasius
blocks.title: Theosis
blocks.body:
Athanasius gives the most famous summary of the patristic gospel: the Word became human so that we might be made divine. He means that by union with the incarnate Son we share God's life and incorruption by grace, never becoming God by nature.

In the *Orations against the Arians* he ties this to adoption: we become sons by grace because the true Son took our flesh.

blocks.subject: person:athanasius
blocks.title: Trinity: God named as Father
blocks.body: Against Arius, Athanasius argues that the Son is eternally from the Father's own being, not a creature. He adds that it is more fitting to name God from the Son, as *Father*, than from his works as "Unoriginate" or Maker. God's first name, for Athanasius, is relational.

blocks.subject: person:gregory-of-nyssa
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Gregory was the younger brother of Basil of Caesarea and bishop of Nyssa in Cappadocia from about 372. He was a leading voice at the Council of Constantinople (381). His writings range from doctrine (*The Great Catechism*, *Against Eunomius*) to spiritual theology (*The Life of Moses*) and reflections on death and resurrection.

blocks.subject: person:gregory-of-nyssa
blocks.title: Atonement: the ransom and the healing
blocks.body:
Gregory tells the ransom story vividly: the devil, seeing the Son's humanity, took the bait and was caught by the hidden divinity, like a fish on a hook. He insists the deception was just and even healing, because the same act will finally benefit the deceiver too.

Behind the image is a medical vision: God acts as a physician who removes evil from human nature by uniting it to himself.

blocks.subject: person:gregory-of-nyssa
blocks.title: Endless growth in God
blocks.body: For Gregory, perfection is not a finished state but endless progress: since God is infinite, the soul can always go further into him. Following God wherever he leads is itself the vision of God. This "ever-advancing" union (often called *epektasis*, from Php 3:13) is his picture of theosis.

citations.ref: Life of Moses, Book 1 (prologue) and Book 2 (conclusion)

blocks.subject: person:gregory-of-nyssa
blocks.title: Restoration of all
blocks.body: Gregory hoped that evil, being finite and parasitic, will at last be emptied out, and that every creature will finally be restored to God, with purifying judgement serving that end. This hope is a minority view, debated in his time and since.

citations.ref: On the Soul and the Resurrection

blocks.subject: person:gregory-of-nyssa
blocks.title: Trinity: one activity
blocks.body: Answering the charge that three Persons means three gods, Gregory argues that every act of God toward creation begins from the Father, proceeds through the Son and is completed in the Spirit. One shared life and one action show one God.

blocks.subject: person:gregory-of-nazianzus
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Gregory, called "the Theologian" in the East, was a friend of Basil from student days in Athens. In 379–381 he led the small Nicene congregation in Constantinople, where his five *Theological Orations* defended the full deity of the Son and the Spirit. He briefly presided at the Council of Constantinople (381) before resigning and returning to Cappadocia.

blocks.subject: person:gregory-of-nazianzus
blocks.title: What is not assumed is not healed
blocks.body: Against Apollinarius, who denied Christ a human mind, Gregory wrote that what the Son did not take up he did not heal. Salvation works by union: Christ heals human nature by taking all of it, mind included, into himself.

blocks.subject: person:gregory-of-nazianzus
blocks.title: To whom was the ransom paid?
blocks.body: Gregory asks the question directly. Not to the evil one, which would be outrageous; nor to the Father, who did not hold us captive and did not delight in the blood of his Son. The Father accepted the sacrifice by his own plan, so that humanity might be sanctified by the humanity of God. Gregory's answer undercuts both a crude ransom-to-Satan view and the idea that the Father needed to be paid.

blocks.subject: person:gregory-of-nazianzus
blocks.title: Trinity
blocks.body: In the *Theological Orations* Gregory defends the one Godhead in three Persons, with the Father as source, the Son begotten and the Spirit proceeding. He explains why the Spirit's deity was revealed gradually in Scripture: God taught his people step by step, as they were able to bear it.

blocks.subject: person:origen
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Origen led the catechetical school in Alexandria and later taught in Caesarea in Palestine. He was the most prolific scholar of the early church: commentaries, homilies, the *Hexapla* (a six-column Old Testament), and *On First Principles*, the first attempt at a systematic theology. He was tortured in the Decian persecution and died soon after, around 253. Some of his speculative ideas were condemned long after his death.

blocks.subject: person:origen
blocks.title: Ransom to the powers
blocks.body: Origen is an early source of the ransom theory: Christ gave his life as a ransom to the one who held us captive, the evil one, who could not hold him. The cross is God's liberation of captives.

blocks.subject: person:origen
blocks.title: Christ is the kingdom
blocks.body: Origen calls Christ *autobasileia*, the kingdom itself. Where Jesus is, the reign of God is present. This gives the kingdom a personal, present centre rather than a merely future one.

blocks.subject: person:origen
blocks.title: Trinity: eternal generation
blocks.body: Origen taught that the Son is begotten from the Father eternally, as brightness from light, so there was never a time when the Father was without the Son. Some of his language also ranks the Son below the Father, which later debates had to correct.

blocks.subject: person:origen
blocks.title: Restoration
blocks.body: Origen held that the end will be like the beginning: God's purpose is to bring all rational creatures back to himself, with judgement acting as a refining fire. This was contested in his own time and condemned in later Origenist controversies.

blocks.subject: person:clement-of-alexandria
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Clement taught in Alexandria in the late second century, before Origen. A convert well read in Greek philosophy and poetry, he presented Christ as the true Teacher who leads humanity from paganism to knowledge of God. His trilogy is the *Exhortation*, the *Instructor* and the *Stromata*. He left Alexandria during persecution around 202.

blocks.subject: person:clement-of-alexandria
blocks.title: The Word became human so we might become divine
blocks.body: Clement's *Exhortation* already uses the exchange formula: the Word of God became human so that you might learn from a human how a human may become God. Union with God is the end of the Christian life.

blocks.subject: person:clement-of-alexandria
blocks.title: God as loving Tutor
blocks.body: In *The Instructor* Christ is the Tutor of God's children, and believers are "little children" enlightened in baptism. Clement argues that God's correction is the action of a loving father and physician, aimed at healing, not revenge.

blocks.subject: person:clement-of-alexandria
blocks.title: Corrective judgement
blocks.body: Clement held that God's punishments are remedial and that the gospel was preached even to the dead (1 Pet 3:19). He is an early witness to the hope that judgement serves restoration.

blocks.subject: person:justin-martyr
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Justin was born in Flavia Neapolis in Samaria, studied philosophy, and became a Christian teacher in Rome. His *Apologies* defend Christians to the emperor; his *Dialogue with Trypho* argues from the Hebrew Scriptures with a Jewish teacher. He was beheaded in Rome around 165.

blocks.subject: person:justin-martyr
blocks.title: The Logos in all people
blocks.body: Justin taught that the Word (*Logos*) who became flesh in Jesus had already sown "seeds" of truth among all people. Whatever any thinker said well belongs to Christians, because it came from the Word. Christ is the full presence of what every culture glimpsed in part.

blocks.subject: person:justin-martyr
blocks.title: The Son who appeared to the patriarchs
blocks.body: Justin argued from the Old Testament that "another God and Lord" under the Father appeared to Abraham, Jacob and Moses, and that this was the Word who later became man. He also describes the Word as begotten from the Father like fire kindled from fire, without the Father being diminished.

blocks.subject: person:justin-martyr
blocks.title: Kingdom hope
blocks.body: Justin expected a thousand-year reign in a rebuilt Jerusalem, but admitted that many true Christians did not share this view. His honesty shows that early eschatology was not uniform.

blocks.subject: person:ignatius
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Ignatius was bishop of Antioch. Around 110 (the date is debated) he was taken under guard to Rome to die in the arena, and on the way wrote seven letters to churches in Asia Minor, to Rome and to Polycarp. They are among the earliest Christian writings after the New Testament.

blocks.subject: person:ignatius
blocks.title: One physician
blocks.body: Ignatius calls Jesus the one Physician, both fleshly and spiritual, born and unborn, God in man, true life in death. Salvation is healing through union with the incarnate Lord, and the Eucharist is the "medicine of immortality".

blocks.subject: person:ignatius
blocks.title: The old kingdom destroyed
blocks.body: Ignatius describes the star of the nativity shining out so that magic was dissolved, ignorance removed and the "ancient kingdom" destroyed, because God appeared in human form for the newness of eternal life. The incarnation is the beginning of Christ's victory over the powers.

blocks.subject: person:ignatius
blocks.title: Union with Christ and the Father
blocks.body: Ignatius urges the churches to be united with the bishop and with one another as Christ is united with the Father. Unity in the church mirrors the unity of the Father and the Son.

blocks.subject: person:augustine
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Augustine was born in Thagaste in North Africa in 354, taught rhetoric in Carthage, Rome and Milan, and was baptised by Ambrose in 387. He became bishop of Hippo in 395/396 and wrote until his death in 430 as the Vandals besieged the city. His *Confessions*, *City of God* and *On the Trinity* shaped Western theology more than any other writer after Paul.

blocks.subject: person:augustine
blocks.title: Made for God
blocks.body: Augustine opens the *Confessions* by saying that God made us for himself, and our heart is restless until it rests in him. His whole theology is driven by love and desire for God. In a sermon he also uses the patristic exchange: God became human so that humans might become gods (by grace).

blocks.subject: person:augustine
blocks.title: The devil overcome by justice
blocks.body: Augustine taught that Christ defeated the devil not by power first but by justice: the devil, by killing the sinless one over whom he had no claim, lost his hold over those who belong to Christ. This is a form of the ransom/victory view.

blocks.subject: person:augustine
blocks.title: Original sin and the guilt of Adam
blocks.body: Augustine taught that all humanity was present in Adam and that his sin brought both death and guilt to all his descendants, so that even infants need the grace of baptism. Reading Rom 5:12 in the Latin *in quo* ("in whom all sinned"), he made this the backbone of Western teaching on sin and grace. This is the root of the later legal reading; Eastern Fathers generally did not follow him on inherited guilt.

citations.ref: On the Merits and Remission of Sins 1.10-11

blocks.subject: person:augustine
blocks.title: Trinity as love
blocks.body: In *On the Trinity* Augustine seeks images of the Trinity in the human mind (memory, understanding, will) and names the Holy Spirit as the mutual love and gift of the Father and the Son.

blocks.subject: person:augustine
blocks.title: The kingdom now: the church's age
blocks.body: Augustine read the thousand years of Rev 20 as the present age of the church, in which Christ already reigns with his saints and Satan is bound. This turned the West away from earthly millennialism and is a root of both amillennial and postmillennial readings.

blocks.subject: person:john-chrysostom
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: John, later called *Chrysostom* ("golden-mouthed"), was a preacher in Antioch for twelve years and became archbishop of Constantinople in 398. His verse-by-verse homilies on Matthew, John, Paul's letters and Hebrews are the largest body of patristic preaching. He offended the court with his preaching on wealth and died in exile in 407.

blocks.subject: person:john-chrysostom
blocks.title: Romans 5: death, not inherited guilt
blocks.body: On Rom 5:12–19, Chrysostom explains that through Adam's fall all became mortal, and "made sinners" means liable to suffering and death, not personally guilty of Adam's act. Grace in Christ overflows far beyond the harm Adam caused. This is the typical Eastern reading, different from Augustine's.

blocks.subject: person:john-chrysostom
blocks.title: Hell is despoiled
blocks.body: The Easter (Paschal) homily traditionally attributed to Chrysostom, still read in Orthodox churches at Pascha, proclaims that Christ entered Hades and despoiled it: death's sting is gone, Hades is embittered, Christ is risen and life reigns. It is the classic liturgical voice of Christus Victor.

blocks.subject: person:john-chrysostom
blocks.title: Union in John's Gospel
blocks.body: Preaching on John's Gospel, Chrysostom stresses that the Word who became flesh is one with the Father and that through him believers receive the right to become children of God (John 1:12).

blocks.subject: person:maximus-the-confessor
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Maximus was a Byzantine monk who opposed the imperial compromise that Christ had only one will. He insisted that Christ had a fully human will freely united to the divine. For this his tongue and right hand were cut off, and he died in exile in 662. The Third Council of Constantinople (680–681) vindicated his teaching.

blocks.subject: person:maximus-the-confessor
blocks.title: Creation made for union
blocks.body: For Maximus the incarnation was not merely a repair after the fall: it is the "great and hidden mystery", the goal for which all things were made. In Christ, God and humanity are united without confusion, and every creature is drawn toward that union.

blocks.subject: person:maximus-the-confessor
blocks.title: Theosis and the logoi
blocks.body: Maximus teaches that each creature has its *logos*, its meaning in the Word. Human beings are called to unite in love what was divided (heaven and earth, created and uncreated) and so to become by grace what God is by nature.

blocks.subject: person:maximus-the-confessor
blocks.title: Two wills, one obedience
blocks.body: Maximus argued that Christ healed the human will by having one: in Gethsemane his human will freely consented to the Father. Salvation is a real human "yes" to God, achieved in Christ for us.

blocks.subject: person:basil-of-caesarea
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Basil was bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia from 370 to 379. A monastic organiser and social reformer, he built a large complex for the poor and sick outside the city. With his brother Gregory of Nyssa and his friend Gregory of Nazianzus he formed the "Cappadocian Fathers", whose language of one *ousia* (being) and three *hypostases* (persons) shaped the creed of 381.

blocks.subject: person:basil-of-caesarea
blocks.title: The Spirit who makes us like God
blocks.body: In *On the Holy Spirit* Basil describes the Spirit's work: from him comes foreknowledge of the future, understanding of mysteries, abiding in God, likeness to God and, highest of all, being made God. Theosis is the Spirit's gift.

blocks.subject: person:basil-of-caesarea
blocks.title: Trinity: glory to the Father, with the Son, with the Spirit
blocks.body: Basil defended giving glory to the Father "with the Son together with the Holy Spirit", arguing from baptism (Matt 28:19) and worship that the Spirit is ranked with the Father and Son. He explains that honour paid to the image passes to the original, so worshipping the Son is worship of the one God.

blocks.subject: person:basil-of-caesarea
blocks.title: Baptism as death and life
blocks.body: Basil reads baptism as an imitation of Christ's death, burial and rising (Rom 6:3–4), in which the old life is ended and a new one begun by the Spirit.

blocks.subject: person:cyril-of-alexandria
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Cyril was patriarch of Alexandria from 412 to 444. He led the opposition to Nestorius and dominated the Council of Ephesus (431), which affirmed Mary as *Theotokos* (God-bearer). His commentaries on John and Luke and his christological letters became standard for both Chalcedonian and non-Chalcedonian churches.

blocks.subject: person:cyril-of-alexandria
blocks.title: One Christ, one subject
blocks.body: Cyril insisted that the eternal Word himself was born, suffered in the flesh and rose. There are not two "sons" but one incarnate Word. Because God himself has united our nature to himself, salvation is real union.

blocks.subject: person:cyril-of-alexandria
blocks.title: Sons by grace
blocks.body: Commenting on John 1:12–14, Cyril explains that the Son by nature became man so that we, by nature creatures, might become sons by grace through the Spirit. On John 17:21 he teaches that our union with God comes through the Son's flesh and the Spirit's indwelling.

blocks.subject: person:ephrem-the-syrian
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Ephrem was born in Nisibis (modern Nusaybin, Turkey) around 306 and served as a deacon and teacher there. When the city was ceded to Persia in 363 he moved to Edessa, where he died in 373 while caring for victims of famine. He wrote hundreds of *madrāshê* (teaching hymns) in Syriac, sung by women's choirs he trained. He represents a Semitic, poetic Christianity outside the Greek and Latin worlds.

blocks.subject: person:ephrem-the-syrian
blocks.title: The great exchange
blocks.body: Ephrem sings of the incarnation as a wondrous exchange: the Lord took what is ours so that we might receive what is his. He gave us his divinity, and we gave him our humanity.

blocks.subject: person:ephrem-the-syrian
blocks.title: The robe of glory
blocks.body: A central image for Ephrem is clothing. Adam and Eve were clothed in a robe of glory that was lost in the fall; Christ "put on" Adam's body and, in baptism, believers put on Christ and are clothed again in glory. Salvation is restoration to the life of Paradise.

blocks.subject: person:ephrem-the-syrian
blocks.title: Reverent silence about God
blocks.body: Ephrem opposed those who tried to define God's being by debate. God reveals himself in Scripture's names and symbols, and the right response is faith and praise, not curiosity that scrutinises the Son.

blocks.subject: person:polycarp
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Polycarp was bishop of Smyrna in Asia Minor. Irenaeus, who knew him as a boy, says he had been taught by apostles, especially John. He visited Rome around 155 to discuss the date of Easter with bishop Anicetus. Soon after he was burned in Smyrna, saying (according to the *Martyrdom of Polycarp*) that he had served Christ for eighty-six years. His *Letter to the Philippians* survives.

blocks.subject: person:polycarp
blocks.title: Christ who loosed the pangs of death
blocks.body: Polycarp's letter begins with Christ, who for our sins endured even death and whom God raised, loosing the pangs of Hades (Acts 2:24). Believers trust the God who raised him and so share his life.

blocks.subject: person:polycarp
blocks.title: He endured all things that we might live
blocks.body: Quoting 1 Pet 2:22–24, Polycarp says Christ bore our sins in his own body on the tree and endured all things for us, that we might live in him. He then calls the church to imitate his patience. The atonement here is participation: we live in him and follow him.

blocks.subject: person:polycarp
blocks.title: Prayer to the Father through the Son
blocks.body: The prayer attributed to Polycarp at his death blesses the Father of the beloved Son Jesus Christ and gives glory to the Father through Christ, with the Holy Spirit. It is one of the earliest Trinitarian doxologies outside Scripture.

blocks.subject: person:clement-of-rome
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Clement led the church in Rome at the end of the first century. The letter called *1 Clement*, sent from the Roman church to Corinth around 96 (some date it earlier), urges the Corinthians to end a dispute that had removed their elders. It praises love as the bond of union with God.

blocks.subject: person:clement-of-rome
blocks.title: Love that binds us to God
blocks.body: *1 Clement* praises love as the bond that unites us to God and says the Lord gave his blood for us by the will of God, his flesh for our flesh and his life for our lives. Its long closing prayer addresses God as the Creator and Father who heals and saves.

blocks.subject: person:melito-of-sardis
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Melito was bishop of Sardis in Asia Minor in the later second century and a Quartodeciman, keeping Pascha on 14 Nisan. His sermon *On Pascha* was rediscovered in the twentieth century. It reads the Exodus lamb as a type of Christ and ends with Christ proclaiming his victory over death.

blocks.subject: person:melito-of-sardis
blocks.title: Christ the true Passover
blocks.body: In *On Pascha* Melito reads Israel's Passover as a model pointing to Christ, the true Lamb. The sermon ends with the risen Christ declaring that he has destroyed death, trampled Hades and bound the strong one, inviting all to receive forgiveness. It also contains a harsh accusation against Israel that later fed Christian anti-Judaism.

blocks.subject: person:hippolytus
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Hippolytus was a presbyter in Rome in the early third century who clashed with its bishops over discipline and Christology. Exiled to Sardinia with bishop Pontian in 235, he is honoured as a martyr. *The Refutation of All Heresies* and *On Christ and Antichrist* are attributed to him; the *Apostolic Tradition* traditionally linked to him is debated.

blocks.subject: person:cyprian
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Cyprian, a wealthy rhetorician converted in mid-life, became bishop of Carthage around 248. He hid during the Decian persecution (250) and afterwards had to decide how to restore Christians who had lapsed. *On the Unity of the Church* argues that there is one church with one episcopate. He was beheaded in 258 under Valerian.

blocks.subject: person:cyril-of-jerusalem
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Cyril was bishop of Jerusalem from about 350, exiled several times in the Arian disputes. His *Catechetical Lectures*, given to candidates for baptism in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, show fourth-century teaching on the creed, baptism and the Eucharist.

blocks.subject: person:cyril-of-jerusalem
blocks.title: Test my teaching by Scripture
blocks.body: Cyril tells his catechumens not to believe even him unless what he says is proved from the divine Scriptures, because the faith rests on demonstration from Scripture, not on clever speech.

blocks.subject: person:ambrose
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Ambrose was the Roman governor in Milan when the people acclaimed him bishop in 374, though he was not yet baptised. He resisted the empress Justina's support for the Arians, made emperor Theodosius do public penance after the massacre at Thessalonica (390), and introduced congregational hymn-singing to the West. His preaching helped convert Augustine.

blocks.subject: person:leo-the-great
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Leo was bishop of Rome from 440 to 461. His letter to Flavian of Constantinople, the *Tome* (449), set out that Christ is one person in two natures, each doing what is proper to it in communion with the other. It was acclaimed at Chalcedon in 451. He also met Attila in 452 and the Vandal king Gaiseric in 455.

blocks.subject: person:benedict-of-nursia
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Benedict left studies in Rome to live as a hermit, then founded monasteries, including Monte Cassino around 529. His *Rule* balances prayer, work and study under an abbot ("father"), and became the standard for Western monasticism. Most of what is known of his life comes from Gregory the Great's *Dialogues*, Book 2.

blocks.subject: person:gregory-the-great
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Gregory, son of a Roman senatorial family, was prefect of Rome, became a monk and was elected bishop of Rome in 590 during plague and Lombard invasion. He organised famine relief, wrote the *Pastoral Rule* and *Dialogues*, and in 596 sent Augustine (later of Canterbury) to the English.

blocks.subject: person:symeon-the-new-theologian
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Symeon was a monk in Constantinople and abbot of the monastery of St Mamas. He taught that the Christian life involves conscious experience of the Holy Spirit and the vision of God as light. He was exiled after conflict with church authorities and died in 1022. His *Hymns of Divine Love* describe that experience.

blocks.subject: person:symeon-the-new-theologian
blocks.title: Seeing the divine light
blocks.body: In his hymns Symeon describes being united to Christ and seeing God as uncreated light. He insists this is not a privilege for a few ascetics but the normal inheritance of the baptised.

blocks.subject: person:gregory-palamas
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Gregory Palamas was a monk of Mount Athos and later archbishop of Thessalonica. In the 1330s–1340s he defended the hesychasts, monks who prayed the Jesus Prayer and claimed to see the uncreated light of Tabor, against the scholar Barlaam. Councils in Constantinople (1341, 1351) upheld his teaching.

blocks.subject: person:gregory-palamas
blocks.title: Essence and energies
blocks.body: Palamas distinguished God's unknowable essence from his uncreated energies, by which God truly gives himself. We never become God's essence, but we really share God's own life and light. This is his account of how theosis is possible.

blocks.subject: person:francis-of-assisi
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Francis, son of a cloth merchant in Assisi, renounced his inheritance around 1206 to live in poverty, rebuild ruined churches and serve lepers. His brotherhood was approved by Pope Innocent III in 1209/1210. He preached to the Sultan al-Kamil in Egypt in 1219 during the Fifth Crusade. Near the end of his life he wrote the *Canticle of the Creatures*.

blocks.subject: person:julian-of-norwich
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Julian was an anchoress attached to St Julian's church in Norwich. In May 1373, during a severe illness, she received sixteen visions (she called them "showings") of Christ's passion and God's love. She wrote a short account and, after decades of reflection, a long version. Little else is known of her life.

blocks.subject: person:julian-of-norwich
blocks.title: No wrath in God
blocks.body: Julian reports that in her showings she saw no anger in God; the wrath is on our side, not his. She also speaks of Christ as our Mother, and of God's assurance that all shall be well.

blocks.subject: person:erasmus
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Erasmus of Rotterdam was the leading humanist scholar of the early sixteenth century. In 1516 he published the first printed Greek New Testament to go on sale, with a new Latin translation and notes. Luther used it for his German New Testament and Tyndale for his English one. Erasmus criticised church abuses but did not join the Reformation, and debated Luther on free will (1524–1525).

blocks.subject: person:ulrich-zwingli
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Zwingli became preacher at the Great Minster in Zürich in 1519 and preached straight through the Gospel of Matthew. In 1523 the city council adopted his *Sixty-seven Articles* after a public disputation. He held that the Lord's Supper is a memorial and broke with Luther at Marburg (1529). He died as a chaplain at the battle of Kappel in 1531.

blocks.subject: person:menno-simons
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Menno Simons was a Catholic priest in Friesland who left the church in 1536 to join the peaceful Anabaptists after the violent Münster episode. He spent the rest of his life as a hunted travelling elder, gathering communities committed to adult baptism, non-resistance and discipleship.

blocks.subject: person:menno-simons
blocks.title: Discipleship and the new birth
blocks.body: Menno taught that true faith is a living new birth that changes how one lives, and that the church is a community of disciples baptised on confession of faith who refuse the sword.

blocks.subject: person:jacobus-arminius
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Arminius studied at Leiden and Geneva (under Beza) and became professor at Leiden in 1603. He questioned unconditional election and taught that God's grace can be resisted. After his death in 1609 his followers issued the *Remonstrance* (1610), which the Synod of Dort rejected in 1618–1619.

blocks.subject: person:jacobus-arminius
blocks.title: Grace for all
blocks.body: In his *Declaration of Sentiments* Arminius sets out his objections to supralapsarian predestination and argues that God's decree to save is in Christ, for those who believe, and that grace is offered sincerely to all.

blocks.subject: person:john-wesley
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: John Wesley was an Anglican priest and Oxford fellow. After a failed mission to Georgia, he felt his "heart strangely warmed" at a meeting in Aldersgate Street, London, on 24 May 1738. From 1739 he preached in the open air and organised converts into societies, classes and bands, travelling some 250,000 miles on horseback. Methodism separated from the Church of England only after his death.

blocks.subject: person:john-wesley
blocks.title: Christian perfection as perfect love
blocks.body: Wesley taught that the goal of salvation is not only pardon but holiness: the love of God and neighbour filling the heart. He called this "Christian perfection" or "perfect love", and drew partly on Eastern writers such as Macarius and Ephrem.

citations.ref: A Plain Account of Christian Perfection

blocks.subject: person:george-whitefield
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Whitefield, an Anglican priest and member of the Oxford "Holy Club" with the Wesleys, became the most famous preacher of the eighteenth century. He made seven trips to the American colonies, where his open-air preaching from 1739–1740 was central to the First Great Awakening. Unlike Wesley he was a Calvinist. He died in Newburyport, Massachusetts, in 1770.

blocks.subject: person:charles-finney
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Finney was a lawyer in upstate New York who was converted in 1821 and became the leading revivalist of the Second Great Awakening. He used "new measures" such as the anxious bench and protracted meetings, taught that revival is the right use of means, and later became president of Oberlin College, which admitted women and Black students.

blocks.subject: person:charles-finney
blocks.title: Revival as the right use of means
blocks.body: In his *Lectures on Revivals of Religion* (1835) Finney argued that a revival is not a miracle but the result of the right use of God-appointed means, a sharp break from the Calvinist view that revival waits on God's sovereign timing.

citations.ref: Lectures on Revivals of Religion, Lecture 1

blocks.subject: person:john-nelson-darby
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Darby was an Anglican curate in County Wicklow, Ireland, who left the established church and became a leading figure among the Brethren from the late 1820s. At the Powerscourt conferences (1831–1833) and afterwards he developed a system that separated God's plan for Israel from his plan for the church, with a secret "rapture" of the church before a future tribulation. He spread it through travels in Europe and North America (1862–1877) and translated the Bible into several languages.

blocks.subject: person:ci-scofield
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Cyrus Ingerson Scofield was a lawyer and Civil War veteran who was converted in 1879 and became a Congregational pastor in Dallas. Influenced by Darby's ideas through the Niagara Bible Conference and James H. Brookes, he produced the *Scofield Reference Bible* (Oxford University Press, 1909; revised 1917), whose notes taught dispensationalism to millions.

blocks.subject: person:ci-scofield
blocks.title: Seven dispensations
blocks.body: Scofield's notes define a dispensation as a period of time in which humanity is tested in respect of obedience to some specific revelation of God's will, and set out seven of them, from Innocence to the Kingdom. They also teach a sharp distinction between Israel and the church.

citations.ref: Scofield Reference Bible, note on Gen 1:28

blocks.subject: person:karl-barth
blocks.title: Life and setting
blocks.body: Barth was a Swiss Reformed pastor whose commentary on Romans (1919, revised 1922) broke with liberal theology. He taught in Germany until expelled in 1935, was the main author of the Barmen Declaration (1934) against the Nazi-controlled church, and spent the rest of his career in Basel writing the unfinished *Church Dogmatics*.

blocks.subject: person:karl-barth
blocks.title: Election in Jesus Christ
blocks.body: Barth reworked the Reformed doctrine of predestination: Jesus Christ is both the electing God and the elected human. In him God chooses humanity for himself and takes rejection upon himself. Election is the sum of the gospel, not a dark decree behind it.

blocks.subject: entry:timeline/council-of-jerusalem
blocks.body:
Acts 15 describes a meeting in Jerusalem after believers from Judea taught that Gentiles must be circumcised to be saved. Peter recalls the Spirit given to Cornelius' household; Paul and Barnabas report God's work among the nations; James cites Amos 9:11–12 on the rebuilding of David's tent so that the nations seek the Lord.

The letter sent to Antioch asks Gentiles to avoid food offered to idols, blood, what is strangled and sexual immorality, and lays no further burden. The decision kept one table for Jews and Gentiles in the Messiah's family. How Galatians 2 relates to Acts 15 (the same visit or an earlier one) is debated.

blocks.subject: entry:timeline/temple-destroyed
blocks.body:
The Roman siege under Titus ended with the burning of the Temple in the summer of 70; Josephus (*Jewish War*, Book 6) describes it. Jesus had wept over the city and warned that not one stone would be left on another within "this generation" (Matt 24:2, 24:34; Luke 19:41–44).

Partial-preterist readers, including many postmillennialists, take much of the Olivet Discourse as fulfilled in these events, while still expecting a future bodily return of Christ. Others read the discourse as wholly or partly future.

blocks.subject: entry:timeline/gospels-written
blocks.body: Most scholars date Mark around 65–70, Matthew and Luke in the 80s and John in the 90s. A minority, following J. A. T. Robinson's *Redating the New Testament* (1976), argues that all four Gospels were written before the fall of Jerusalem in 70, mainly because none describes it as past.

blocks.subject: entry:timeline/nicaea-325
blocks.body: Constantine called bishops to Nicaea in Bithynia in 325. Against Arius, who taught that "there was when the Son was not", the council confessed the Son "begotten, not made, of one being (*homoousios*) with the Father". It also issued canons on church order and settled a common date for Easter. Only a few bishops refused to sign, but the debate over the Nicene faith lasted another half-century.

blocks.subject: entry:timeline/constantinople-381
blocks.body: Called by Theodosius I, the council confirmed the faith of Nicaea and produced (or endorsed) the creed now recited as the Nicene Creed, which confesses the Holy Spirit "the Lord, the giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified". Gregory of Nazianzus presided for a time before resigning.

blocks.subject: entry:timeline/ephesus-431
blocks.body: Nestorius objected to calling Mary *Theotokos* (God-bearer), preferring *Christotokos*. Cyril of Alexandria argued that this split Christ into two subjects. The council at Ephesus, opened by Cyril before the Antiochene bishops arrived, deposed Nestorius. A reconciliation, the Formula of Reunion, followed in 433.

citations.ref: Second and Third Letters to Nestorius

blocks.subject: entry:timeline/chalcedon-451
blocks.body: The council at Chalcedon confessed one and the same Christ, perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity, "in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation". Leo's Tome was received as agreeing with Cyril. Many in Egypt and Syria heard "two natures" as Nestorian and rejected the council, leading to the Oriental Orthodox churches.

blocks.subject: entry:timeline/great-schism-1054
blocks.body: On 16 July 1054 Cardinal Humbert laid a bull of excommunication against Patriarch Michael Cerularius on the altar of Hagia Sophia; the patriarch's synod replied in kind. The issues included papal authority, the *filioque* and leavened versus unleavened bread. Historians stress that the schism was a long process, sealed by the sack of Constantinople in 1204, rather than a single event.

blocks.subject: entry:timeline/cur-deus-homo
