blocks.body: Written in dialogue form with his monk Boso, *Cur Deus Homo* asks why God became man. Anselm answers that sin dishonours God, and either satisfaction or punishment must follow. Only God can make satisfaction, but only a human ought to; so a God-man is needed, whose freely given death more than restores God's honour. Anselm's framework came from feudal ideas of honour and the church's penitential system; it is not yet penal substitution, but it moved Western thought toward a legal reading.

blocks.subject: entry:timeline/ninety-five-theses
blocks.body: Luther, an Augustinian friar and professor at Wittenberg, protested the sale of indulgences preached by Johann Tetzel. His first thesis says that when Jesus said "Repent", he willed the whole life of believers to be repentance. The theses were printed and spread across Germany within weeks.

blocks.subject: entry:timeline/council-of-trent
blocks.body: Meeting in three periods between 1545 and 1563, Trent affirmed Scripture together with unwritten traditions as authoritative, declared the Vulgate authentic, taught justification as both forgiveness and inner renewal by grace with human cooperation, defined seven sacraments, and affirmed purgatory while warning against abuses. It also launched seminaries and reform of clergy.

blocks.subject: entry:timeline/kjv-1611
blocks.body: At the Hampton Court Conference (1604) James I approved a new translation. About fifty scholars in six companies worked from the Hebrew, Greek and earlier English versions, especially Tyndale's. The 1611 edition included the Apocrypha. Its versification became the standard in English Bibles.

blocks.subject: entry:timeline/westminster-confession
blocks.body: The Westminster Assembly, called by the English Parliament during the Civil War, drew up the Confession of Faith (completed 1646), Larger and Shorter Catechisms and a Directory for Public Worship. Its federal (covenant) theology, with a covenant of works with Adam and a covenant of grace in Christ, shaped Presbyterian and many Baptist and Congregationalist confessions.

blocks.subject: entry:timeline/azusa-street
blocks.body: In April 1906 William J. Seymour, a Black Holiness preacher, began meetings in a former church building at 312 Azusa Street, Los Angeles. Black, white, Latino and Asian worshippers prayed together, many speaking in tongues. Visitors carried the message across North America and to Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America within a few years.

blocks.subject: entry:timeline/scofield-bible
blocks.body: The *Scofield Reference Bible* (1909, revised 1917) printed the King James text with headings, cross-references and notes teaching seven dispensations, a distinction between Israel and the church, and a pre-tribulation rapture. It was the main channel through which Darby's system became the default reading of prophecy for many American evangelicals.

citations.ref: Scofield Reference Bible, notes on Gen 1:28 and on dispensations

blocks.subject: entry:timeline/powerscourt-darby
blocks.body: Lady Powerscourt hosted prophecy conferences at her estate in County Wicklow from 1831. J. N. Darby took a leading role. By the mid-1830s he taught that the church is a heavenly people distinct from Israel and will be taken away before the tribulation, when God resumes his dealings with Israel. Possible influences (Edward Irving, Margaret MacDonald's 1830 vision) are debated by historians.

blocks.subject: entry:timeline/vatican-ii
blocks.body: Called by John XXIII and concluded under Paul VI, the council issued sixteen documents. *Sacrosanctum Concilium* allowed the liturgy in local languages; *Dei Verbum* treated Scripture and Tradition as flowing from one source; *Unitatis Redintegratio* spoke of other Christians as brothers and sisters; *Nostra Aetate* rejected holding all Jews responsible for Christ's death.

blocks.subject: entry:timeline/first-great-awakening
blocks.body: Revival began in Jonathan Edwards' church in Northampton, Massachusetts, in 1734–1735 and spread through the colonies with George Whitefield's tours from 1739. It stressed the new birth and personal conversion, crossed denominational lines and split congregations into "New Lights" and "Old Lights".

blocks.subject: entry:timeline/pentecost
blocks.body: At the Jewish feast of Weeks (Shavuot), the disciples were filled with the Spirit and spoke in other languages. Peter explained it as the fulfilment of Joel 2: the last days had begun, Jesus was exalted as Lord and Messiah, and the promise was "to you and your children and to all who are far off" (Acts 2:39).

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/eastern-orthodox
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body:
The Orthodox Church is a family of self-governing (autocephalous) churches in communion with one another, with the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople as "first among equals". It has roughly 200–260 million members, mostly in Eastern Europe, the Middle East and their diasporas.

Worship centres on the Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom. Salvation is described as healing and union with God (*theosis*) through the Son and the Spirit, received in the church's sacramental life.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/eastern-orthodox
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body:
Orthodox Christians trace their church to the apostles and the Greek-speaking churches of the Roman East. The seven ecumenical councils (Nicaea 325 to Nicaea 787) define its doctrine of the Trinity, Christ and icons.

East and West drifted apart over language, the authority of the bishop of Rome and the addition of the *filioque* to the creed. The mutual excommunications of 1054 and the crusaders' sack of Constantinople (1204) sealed the division. In the fourteenth century the councils supporting Gregory Palamas affirmed that believers truly share God's uncreated energies.

After the fall of Constantinople (1453) most Orthodox lived under Ottoman rule, while Russia became the largest Orthodox nation. Orthodox theology never adopted Augustine's doctrine of inherited guilt or Anselm's satisfaction theory, and it reads the cross chiefly as Christ's victory over death and the healing of human nature.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/oriental-orthodox
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: The Oriental Orthodox family includes the Coptic Orthodox Church of Egypt, the Syriac Orthodox Church, the Armenian Apostolic Church, the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches and the Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church of India. They recognise one another but are not in communion with the Eastern Orthodox or Rome.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/oriental-orthodox
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body:
These churches accept Nicaea, Constantinople and Ephesus, and follow Cyril of Alexandria's formula of "one incarnate nature of God the Word". They rejected Chalcedon's "in two natures" as sounding Nestorian. Their opponents called them "Monophysites"; they prefer "Miaphysite", stressing one united nature, fully divine and fully human, without mixture.

Political conflicts with Byzantium and later life under Islamic rule hardened the separation. Since the 1960s official dialogues with Eastern Orthodox and Catholic theologians have concluded that both sides confess the same faith about Christ in different words.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/church-of-the-east
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: The Church of the East today survives mainly as the Assyrian Church of the East and the Ancient Church of the East, with communities in Iraq, Iran, Syria and the diaspora; the Chaldean Catholic Church is its branch in communion with Rome.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/church-of-the-east
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body:
Christianity in Mesopotamia and Persia grew outside the Roman Empire. At the Synod of Seleucia-Ctesiphon (410) the Persian church organised itself and accepted the Nicene Creed. It did not accept the Council of Ephesus (431), followed the Antiochene theology of Theodore of Mopsuestia, and was later labelled "Nestorian", a name it rejects.

Its monks reached China by 635 (recorded on the Xi'an Stele of 781) and Central Asia, India and Mongolia. Mongol and Timurid upheaval in the fourteenth century devastated it. In 1994 Pope John Paul II and Patriarch Mar Dinkha IV signed a common declaration affirming that their churches share the same faith in Christ.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/roman-catholic
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: The Catholic Church comprises the Latin Church and more than twenty Eastern Catholic churches, all in communion with the bishop of Rome. It teaches through Scripture and Tradition, interpreted by the bishops in communion with the pope.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/roman-catholic
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body:
Catholics trace their church to the apostles and the early church in Rome. The Latin West developed its own emphases: Augustine's doctrine of original sin and grace, the penitential system that shaped Anselm's satisfaction theory, scholastic theology (Aquinas), and the papacy's growing jurisdiction.

The Council of Trent (1545–1563) answered the Reformation by defining justification, the sacraments, Scripture and Tradition, and purgatory. Vatican I (1870) defined papal infallibility; Vatican II (1962–1965) reformed the liturgy and opened dialogue with other Christians and religions.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/eastern-catholic
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: More than twenty churches, such as the Ukrainian Greek Catholic, Maronite, Melkite, Chaldean and Syro-Malabar churches, keep Eastern liturgies and spirituality while recognising the pope.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/eastern-catholic
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body: Most came about when parts of Orthodox or Oriental churches entered union with Rome, for example the Union of Brest (1596) in Ukraine and Belarus. The Maronites of Lebanon have no separate Orthodox counterpart. Their existence remains sensitive in Catholic–Orthodox relations, where the method of "uniatism" was disowned in the Balamand statement (1993).

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/lutheran
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: Lutherans number roughly 75 million worldwide, strongest in Germany, Scandinavia, the United States, Tanzania, Ethiopia and Indonesia. They keep a liturgical worship and confess the Book of Concord.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/lutheran
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body:
Luther's protest against indulgences (1517) grew into a reform centred on justification by faith. Melanchthon's Augsburg Confession (1530) and the Book of Concord (1580) defined Lutheran teaching.

Luther's own language mixes forensic and participatory themes: he spoke of a "joyful exchange" in which Christ takes our sin and we receive his righteousness, and of Christ present in faith. Later Lutheran orthodoxy stressed forensic, imputed righteousness. Finnish Lutheran scholars since the 1970s have argued that Luther also taught real participation in Christ, close to theosis; that reading is debated.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/reformed-presbyterian
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: The Reformed family includes Presbyterians (Scotland, the US, Korea), Dutch and Swiss Reformed churches and many united churches. Government is by elders in local sessions, presbyteries and synods.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/reformed-presbyterian
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body:
The Reformed tradition began in Zürich (Zwingli, 1523) and Geneva (Calvin, from 1536/1541) and spread to France, the Netherlands, Scotland (Knox, 1560) and England. Calvin's Institutes taught that Christ bore the punishment of sin in our place, alongside a strong theme of union with Christ.

Later Reformed orthodoxy hardened predestination (Beza), defined limited atonement at Dort (1619) and developed federal theology with a covenant of works and a covenant of grace (Westminster, 1646). Nineteenth-century Princeton (Hodge, Warfield) made penal substitution the centre of the gospel. In the twentieth century Karl Barth and the Torrance brothers reworked the tradition around God's self-giving in Christ and the Trinity's life.

citations.ref: Systematic Theology, vol. 2 (on the satisfaction of Christ)

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/anglican
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: Anglicans (Episcopalians in the US and Scotland) hold together catholic order (bishops, liturgy, sacraments) and Reformation doctrine. The Archbishop of Canterbury is a focus of unity but has no jurisdiction outside England.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/anglican
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body:
Henry VIII broke with Rome in 1534 over his marriage; Archbishop Cranmer then reformed worship in English (Book of Common Prayer, 1549 and 1552). After Mary I's Catholic restoration, the Elizabethan Settlement (1559) and the Thirty-Nine Articles (1571) set a moderate Protestant course.

Puritans pushed for further reform; the Oxford Movement (from 1833) recovered catholic and patristic emphases. Anglican divines read the Greek Fathers widely, and Anglican theology has often held penal and participatory themes side by side. The Communion spread with the British Empire and today is largest in Africa.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/anabaptist-mennonite
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: Mennonites number about 2 million worldwide, with large churches in Congo, Ethiopia, India and the Americas. Related groups include the Amish and Hutterites.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/anabaptist-mennonite
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body:
In Zürich in January 1525 Conrad Grebel and others baptised one another as believers, rejecting infant baptism and state control of the church. Catholics and Protestants alike persecuted them; thousands were executed. The Schleitheim Confession (1527) set out believer's baptism, discipline, separation from the world and refusal of the sword.

After the violent Münster episode (1534–1535), Menno Simons gathered peaceful Anabaptists in the Netherlands. Anabaptist theology reads the cross as the pattern of non-violent, enemy-loving discipleship, and many modern Mennonite theologians question violent readings of the atonement in favour of Christus Victor and restorative justice.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/baptist
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: Baptists are one of the largest Protestant families (about 100 million), including the Southern Baptist Convention, Baptist World Alliance members and many independent churches. They range from Calvinistic ("Particular") to Arminian ("General").

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/baptist
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body:
John Smyth's congregation of English exiles in Amsterdam adopted believer's baptism in 1609; Thomas Helwys brought it back to London in 1612 and pleaded for religious liberty for all. "General" Baptists held a general atonement; "Particular" Baptists (from the 1630s) were Calvinist and adopted the Second London Confession (1689), modelled on Westminster.

Baptists grew rapidly in the American revivals and in missions after William Carey (1792). Many American Baptists embraced dispensational premillennialism in the twentieth century.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/methodist
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: Methodism, with about 80 million members including the United Methodist Church, African Methodist Episcopal churches and many national churches, is organised as a "connexion" of churches and conferences.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/methodist
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body:
The Wesley brothers' Holy Club at Oxford (1729) and John Wesley's Aldersgate experience (1738) led to field preaching from 1739 and the organising of converts into societies and classes. American Methodists formed a separate church in 1784; British Methodists separated from the Church of England after John Wesley's death.

Wesley rejected unconditional predestination and taught that grace goes before every person. His goal of salvation was holiness of heart, the restoration of God's image in love, a theme he partly drew from Eastern writers. This makes Methodism close to the relational and therapeutic emphases of the Fathers.

citations.ref: A Plain Account of Christian Perfection

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/quaker
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: Friends today range from unprogrammed silent meetings to evangelical churches with pastors, especially in Kenya, Bolivia and the US. They are known for peace work and abolitionism.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/quaker
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body: George Fox began preaching in 1647; after his vision on Pendle Hill (1652) a movement gathered in northern England. Quakers rejected outward sacraments and paid clergy, refused oaths and hat-honour, and were heavily persecuted under Charles II. William Penn founded Pennsylvania (1681) as a "holy experiment" in religious liberty. Robert Barclay's Apology (1676) gave their theology systematic form.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/congregationalist
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: Congregationalism shaped New England and American higher education (Harvard, Yale). Many Congregational churches merged into the United Church of Christ (1957) and similar unions; others remain independent.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/congregationalist
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body: English Separatists in the late sixteenth century held that each gathered congregation is a complete church. The Pilgrims (1620) and the Massachusetts Bay Puritans (1630) carried this to America, where the Cambridge Platform (1648) defined it. Jonathan Edwards, the leading theologian of the First Great Awakening, was a Congregational pastor. In the nineteenth century New England theology moved toward a "governmental" view of the atonement.

citations.ref: A History of the Work of Redemption

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/pentecostal
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: Classical Pentecostal churches include the Assemblies of God, the Church of God in Christ, the Church of God (Cleveland) and the Foursquare Church. With charismatics, the wider movement counts several hundred million people, mostly in the Global South.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/pentecostal
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body: Pentecostalism grew from the Holiness movement. At Topeka (1901) Charles Parham taught tongues as the "initial evidence" of Spirit baptism; at Azusa Street (1906) William Seymour led an interracial revival that sent missionaries worldwide. Early splits divided "finished work" from Holiness Pentecostals and Trinitarian from Oneness groups (1916). Many Pentecostal churches adopted dispensational eschatology, though some today embrace a more kingdom-now emphasis.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/charismatic
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: The charismatic movement brought Spirit baptism and gifts into Anglican, Lutheran, Catholic and other churches from 1960, and later gave rise to independent networks such as Vineyard (1980s) and many non-denominational churches.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/charismatic
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body: Dennis Bennett's announcement at St Mark's Episcopal Church, Van Nuys (1960), and the Catholic retreat at Duquesne University (1967) began the charismatic renewal. The "Third Wave" (1980s) associated with John Wimber stressed signs and wonders without Pentecostal tongues doctrine. Some charismatic streams teach that God's kingdom advances now through the church, overlapping with postmillennial hopes.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/brethren
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: Brethren assemblies meet without clergy, breaking bread weekly. They divided in 1848 into "Open" Brethren and the "Exclusive" Brethren led by Darby.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/brethren
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body: Small groups in Dublin from about 1827 and in Plymouth from 1831 began meeting for the Lord's Supper outside the established church. J. N. Darby became the dominant teacher. His system distinguished God's earthly people (Israel) from his heavenly people (the church) and taught a secret rapture before the tribulation. Through Bible conferences and the Scofield Reference Bible, Brethren teaching shaped much of global evangelical eschatology.

citations.ref: Scofield Reference Bible, note on Gen 1:28

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/adventist
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: The Seventh-day Adventist Church, formally organised in 1863, has over 20 million members and large education and health networks. It rejects eternal conscious torment, teaching that the wicked are finally destroyed.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/adventist
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body: William Miller predicted Christ's return in 1843–1844. After the "Great Disappointment" of 22 October 1844, a group reinterpreted the date as the beginning of Christ's heavenly ministry of judgement, adopted the seventh-day Sabbath and accepted Ellen G. White's visions. Their teaching of conditional immortality (annihilationism) made them early critics of the doctrine of eternal torment.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/messianic-jewish
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: Messianic congregations exist in Israel, the US, Europe and beyond. Theologies vary widely, from evangelical and Reformed to Torah-observant and independent. In Israel, Hebrew-speaking teachers address both Israelis and the wider church.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/messianic-jewish
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body:
Jewish believers in Jesus have existed since the apostles (Acts 21:20). Modern forerunners include Joseph Rabinowitz's congregation in Kishinev (1880s) and the Hebrew Christian Alliance (1866 in Britain, 1915 in America). After 1967, many young Jewish believers in the Jesus Movement insisted on keeping Jewish identity; the Hebrew Christian Alliance of America renamed itself the Messianic Jewish Alliance in 1975.

Messianic writers often read Scripture through its Jewish setting: covenant, Temple, festivals and Second Temple interpretation. Some, such as Eitan Bar, have challenged imported Western doctrines of atonement and hell from a Jewish perspective.

citations.ref: HELL: A Jewish Perspective on a Christian Doctrine

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/evangelical-free
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: The Evangelical Free Church of America unites churches that agree on central evangelical doctrines while allowing freedom on matters such as the mode of baptism and the timing of the millennium. Trinity Evangelical Divinity School belongs to it.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/evangelical-free
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body: Scandinavian free churches arose from nineteenth-century revivals outside the Lutheran state churches. Immigrant churches in America formed Swedish (1884) and Norwegian-Danish (1884) associations, which merged in 1950. Its 1950 statement of faith originally specified premillennialism; in 2019 it changed this to "glorious" return, opening space for amillennial and postmillennial views.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/restorationist
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: Three main branches came from this movement: the Churches of Christ (a cappella worship), the Christian Churches/Churches of Christ, and the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ).

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/restorationist
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body: Barton Stone's followers (from the Cane Ridge revival of 1801) and Thomas and Alexander Campbell's "Reformers" (Declaration and Address, 1809) united in 1832. They rejected creeds as divisive and sought to follow New Testament patterns. Disagreements over instrumental music and missionary societies divided the movement by 1906.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/holiness
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: Holiness churches include the Church of the Nazarene, the Wesleyan Church, the Free Methodist Church and the Church of God (Anderson). They also fed the Salvation Army and early Pentecostalism.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/holiness
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body: Phoebe Palmer's Tuesday Meetings in New York (from the 1830s) and her "altar theology" taught that believers can be entirely sanctified by consecrating all and trusting God's promise. The National Camp Meeting Association (1867) spread the message; when Methodist leaders resisted, independent Holiness churches formed in the 1880s–1900s.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/moravian
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: The Moravian Church has about one million members, the largest provinces being in Tanzania and South Africa. Its Daily Watchwords (Losungen) are read worldwide.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/moravian
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body: The Unity of the Brethren grew from Jan Hus's followers in Bohemia (1457). Nearly destroyed in the Thirty Years' War, a remnant found refuge on Count Zinzendorf's estate at Herrnhut, where a renewal on 13 August 1727 began a hundred-year prayer watch. From 1732 Moravian missionaries went to the Caribbean, Greenland, North America and South Africa. A Moravian, Peter Böhler, guided John Wesley before Aldersgate.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/waldensian
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: The Waldensian Evangelical Church, united with the Methodists in Italy since 1975, is one of the oldest surviving pre-Reformation movements.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/waldensian
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body: Around 1173 Valdes, a merchant of Lyon, gave away his wealth and began preaching the gospel in the vernacular. Banned for lay preaching and condemned in 1184, the "Poor of Lyon" survived persecution in the Alpine valleys. At the Synod of Chanforan (1532) they adopted Reformed teaching. Massacres followed in 1545 and 1655; religious freedom came in 1848.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/salvation-army
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: The Salvation Army works in over 130 countries, combining evangelism with homeless shelters, addiction recovery and disaster relief.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/salvation-army
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body: William and Catherine Booth began the East London Christian Mission in 1865; it took the name Salvation Army in 1878 and a military-style structure. Catherine Booth championed women's preaching. The Army decided in 1883 not to practise baptism or communion, emphasising inward grace.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/nondenominational-evangelical
blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.body: Non-denominational churches range from small house churches to megachurches, often linked in informal networks. Their theology is usually broadly evangelical, frequently Baptistic in practice and varied in eschatology.

blocks.subject: entry:denomination/nondenominational-evangelical
blocks.title: Origins and how its teaching developed
blocks.body: Independent evangelical churches have existed since the nineteenth century (Bible churches, Moody's Chicago church), but grew rapidly after the Jesus Movement of the late 1960s and the church-growth movement. Calvary Chapel (1965) and Vineyard (1982) began as such networks. Many absorbed dispensational premillennialism through the Scofield Bible and popular prophecy books; others have moved toward kingdom-now and new-creation teaching.

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/original-sin
blocks.title: How the idea developed
blocks.body:
**Before Augustine.** The Fathers agreed that Adam's fall brought death and corruption to all, and that Christ came to heal it. Irenaeus pictured Adam as a child who fell short of maturity; Athanasius described humanity slipping back toward non-being. Tertullian's view that souls are transmitted from parents, and Cyprian's reasoning about infant baptism, prepared Latin thinking for a stronger link between Adam and every person.

**Augustine.** In his controversy with Pelagius (from 411), Augustine argued that all humanity was "in Adam" and sinned in him, so that every child inherits both corruption and guilt. He relied on the Latin translation of Rom 5:12, *in quo omnes peccaverunt* ("in whom all sinned"), where the Greek *eph' hō* more likely means "because" all sinned. Councils at Carthage (418) and Orange (529) adopted his teaching against Pelagianism.

**The East.** Chrysostom and later Orthodox theology read Rom 5 as inherited mortality: because we are mortal, we sin. Orthodoxy speaks of "ancestral sin" and does not teach that infants are guilty of Adam's act.

**Medieval and Reformation West.** Anselm and Aquinas defined original sin as the lack of original justice. The Reformers strengthened Augustine's view into total depravity; Westminster framed it legally as the imputation of Adam's guilt under a covenant of works.

citations.ref: On the Merits and Remission of Sins 1.9-11

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/original-sin
blocks.title: How the legal reading arose
blocks.body:
The legal reading treats the fall as a crime with a verdict: Adam's guilt is legally credited (imputed) to all his descendants, who are therefore under condemnation before they act. Its steps were Augustine's reading of the Latin *in quo* at Rom 5:12, the Latin habit of describing sin as debt and guilt (*reatus*), and Reformed federal theology, which made Adam the legal representative of the race under a covenant of works (Westminster 7.2).

The relational authors read the same texts differently: Rom 5 contrasts two humanities, Adam's and Christ's. What we inherit from Adam is a condition (mortality, alienation, a bent toward sin) more than a court verdict, and Christ the last Adam overcomes it far more fully (Rom 5:15–17).

citations.ref: On the Merits and Remission of Sins 1.10

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/original-sin
blocks.title: How the relational tradition reads it
blocks.body:
Scripture is clear that something went wrong with the whole human family and that we cannot fix ourselves (Rom 3:23). The relational reading frames this as a broken relationship and a sickness unto death, not first as a guilty verdict on newborns.

Jesus is the clearest picture of how God sees sinners: he touched lepers, ate with outcasts and called the lost "son" (Luke 15:24). Paul's point in Rom 5 is not that Adam is stronger than Christ, but that grace "much more" abounds. The Father never stopped being Father; in Christ, the last Adam, humanity is healed from within and restored to sonship (1 Cor 15:22, 45).

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/penal-substitution
blocks.title: How the idea developed
blocks.body:
**Early church.** The Fathers said constantly that Christ died "for us" and "for our sins" (Polycarp quoting 1 Pet 2:24). But their frames were recapitulation, ransom, victory over death and the devil, and the healing of human nature. Some passages (in Eusebius, Athanasius, Augustine) speak of Christ bearing our curse or punishment, and defenders of penal substitution point to them; most historians see these as one strand within a broader participatory picture, not a developed penal theory.

**Anselm (1098).** Anselm argued that sin robs God of honour, and that either satisfaction or punishment must follow. Christ's freely offered life is satisfaction *instead of* punishment.

**The Reformers.** Luther spoke of Christ becoming the greatest sinner and bearing the curse of the law in our place. Calvin taught that Christ bore the weight of God's wrath and, in his soul, the torments of a condemned man (his reading of the descent into hell). Here satisfaction became penal: the punishment itself is transferred.

**After.** Socinus attacked the idea that punishment can be transferred; Grotius answered with a "governmental" theory. Reformed scholastics and the Princeton theologians (Hodge) made penal substitution the centre of the gospel. In the twentieth century Aulén revived Christus Victor, and many writers now criticise penal substitution as distorting the Father's character, while others defend it as biblical.

citations.ref: Defence of the Catholic Faith concerning the Satisfaction of Christ
Systematic Theology, vol. 2 (on the satisfaction of Christ)

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/penal-substitution
blocks.title: How the legal reading arose
blocks.body:
The penal reading grew from three roots: the Latin legal vocabulary of satisfaction and merit (Tertullian, Cyprian, the penitential system); Anselm's feudal logic of honour; and the sixteenth-century courtroom, where justice meant retribution administered by a sovereign. Calvin, trained as a lawyer, framed the cross as a judicial transaction in which the Father's wrath is poured out on the Son.

Relational authors (Aulén, T. F. Torrance, Jersak, Belousek) read the same texts as God's own self-giving: the Father is not appeased by the Son but is "in Christ reconciling the world to himself" (2 Cor 5:19). Isaiah 53 says *we* considered him stricken by God (Isa 53:4); Paul says Christ became a curse to redeem us from the curse (Gal 3:13), the curse of the law's exile and death, which he exhausted by entering it.

citations.ref: Atonement: The Person and Work of Christ

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/penal-substitution
blocks.title: How the relational tradition reads it
blocks.body:
The cross is not the Father punishing the Son, but the Father and Son together, in the Spirit, entering our death to bring us home. "God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself" (2 Cor 5:19). Jesus' words from the cross ("Father, forgive them", Luke 23:34) show the heart of the Father.

Substitution is real: he died our death, "for us". But what he bears is our sin, our curse, our violence and our death, and he defeats them by resurrection (Col 2:15; Heb 2:14–15). This is restorative justice: God's justice puts things right rather than balancing a ledger of pain.

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/penal-substitution
blocks.title: A Jewish-Christian critique
blocks.body: Eitan Bar, an Israeli Jewish follower of Jesus, reads the atonement from within Jewish categories of sacrifice and redemption, and criticises popular preaching that portrays God as violent and abusive toward his Son.

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/eternal-conscious-torment
blocks.title: How the idea developed
blocks.body:
**Jewish background.** Jesus' word *Gehenna* names the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, associated with child sacrifice and judgement (Jer 7:31–32). Second Temple writings use it in different ways: as a place of fiery punishment, of destruction, or of temporary purification. Jesus' hearers did not share a single doctrine of hell.

**Early church.** Justin and Tertullian taught endless punishment; Tertullian even imagined the saints watching. Clement, Origen and Gregory of Nyssa hoped that judgement would purify and that God would finally restore all. Others leaned toward the destruction of the wicked.

**Augustine and the West.** In *City of God* Book 21 Augustine argued against "the merciful" who denied endless punishment, reading *aiōnios* in Matt 25:46 as strictly endless. His view became standard in the West. Origen's teaching on restoration was condemned in the sixth-century Origenist controversies, though the exact force of those anathemas is debated.

**Modern period.** Edwards' revival preaching made hell a motive for conversion. From the nineteenth century, Adventists and others taught conditional immortality; in the twentieth, respected evangelicals such as John Stott leaned that way, and others revived the patristic hope of restoration.

citations.ref: Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/eternal-conscious-torment
blocks.title: How the legal reading arose
blocks.body:
The legal reading treats hell as the sentence of a court: sin against an infinite majesty deserves infinite punishment (Anselm's logic of infinite honour, applied by Aquinas and Edwards). Punishment here is retributive, serving justice for its own sake rather than restoration.

Relational authors ask what kind of Father Jesus reveals. They read Jesus' warnings as real and serious (there is a judgement, and one can refuse love), but question whether endless retributive torment fits the God who "desires all to be saved" (1 Tim 2:4).

citations.ref: Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/eternal-conscious-torment
blocks.title: How the relational tradition reads it
blocks.body:
The relational tradition takes judgement seriously: God's love is a consuming fire (Heb 12:29) that burns away what destroys his children. The question is what that fire is for. Jesus is perfect theology, and he forgives his enemies from the cross.

Within this app's lens, Christians hold different hopes, and they should be stated honestly: conditional immortality (the wicked finally perish), or the hope that the Father's love will finally win every heart (1 Cor 15:28; Col 1:20). What the lens rejects is a picture of the Father as a torturer, which Jesus never shows us. Many of Jesus' Gehenna sayings also warned first-century Israel of the catastrophe of 70 if it refused the way of peace.

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/eternal-conscious-torment
blocks.title: A Jewish perspective
blocks.body: Eitan Bar examines the doctrine of hell from a Jewish perspective, asking how Jesus' Jewish hearers would have understood terms such as Sheol and Gehenna.

citations.ref: HELL: A Jewish Perspective on a Christian Doctrine

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/dispensationalism-and-the-rapture
blocks.title: How the idea developed
blocks.body:
**Early church.** Some second-century Fathers (Papias, Justin, Irenaeus) expected Christ to return and reign a thousand years on earth. None taught a secret rapture years before the visible coming.

**Augustine to the Reformation.** Augustine read Rev 20 as the church age, and this became the main Western view. Many Puritans held a postmillennial hope: the gospel will triumph in history before Christ returns.

**Darby.** In the late 1820s and early 1830s, among the Brethren and at the Powerscourt conferences, J. N. Darby developed a new system: the church is a heavenly people, Israel an earthly one; the prophetic clock stopped at the cross; the church will be removed before Daniel's seventieth week resumes. Possible influences (Lacunza via Edward Irving; the 1830 vision of Margaret MacDonald) are debated.

**America.** Darby's travels, the Niagara conferences and above all the Scofield Reference Bible (1909) made dispensationalism the dominant evangelical eschatology in the US. Popular books in the 1970s–1990s spread it worldwide.

citations.ref: Scofield Reference Bible, note on Gen 1:28

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/dispensationalism-and-the-rapture
blocks.title: How the relational tradition reads it
blocks.body:
The relational, postmillennial reading starts from Jesus: the kingdom has come near in him (Mark 1:15), the stone becomes a mountain that fills the earth (Dan 2:35), and the leaven works through the whole loaf (Matt 13:33). Christ reigns now at the Father's right hand until every enemy is under his feet (1 Cor 15:25).

On this reading, many "end-times" texts warned of the judgement of 70 within "this generation" (Matt 24:34). 1 Thess 4:17 describes believers going out to meet the coming King, as citizens met a visiting emperor and escorted him into their city, not a departure from the earth. God has one family in the Messiah, Jews and Gentiles together (Eph 2:14–16), and his plan is to renew the world, not evacuate it.

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/trinity
blocks.title: How the idea developed
blocks.body:
**Scripture and worship.** The first Christians were Jewish monotheists who prayed to Jesus as Lord and received the Spirit as God's own presence. Baptism was "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matt 28:19).

**Second and third centuries.** Irenaeus described the Son and Spirit as the Father's two hands. Tertullian coined the Latin *trinitas* and the formula "one substance, three persons". Origen taught the Son's eternal generation, though some of his language ranked the Son lower.

**Nicaea and Constantinople.** When Arius taught that the Son was created, Nicaea (325) confessed him *homoousios*, of one being with the Father. Athanasius defended this for decades. The Cappadocians distinguished one *ousia* (being) and three *hypostases* (persons) and defended the Spirit's deity, confirmed at Constantinople (381).

**East and West.** Augustine stressed the unity of God and described the Spirit as the love between Father and Son. The Western addition of *filioque* ("and the Son") to the creed became a major point of division with the East.

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/trinity
blocks.title: How the relational tradition reads it
blocks.body:
The Trinity is the heart of the relational gospel. Before creation there was a Father who loved his Son in the Spirit (John 17:24). Creation and salvation flow out of that shared life, and the gospel is our adoption into it: "that they may be one, as we are one" (John 17:21–23).

Because Jesus is the Father's exact image (Heb 1:3), there is no hidden God behind Jesus with a different face. The cross is not a conflict within God, Father against Son, but the Trinity's one act of self-giving love. The Spirit cries "Abba, Father" in our hearts (Gal 4:6).

citations.ref: Worship, Community and the Triune God of Grace

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/theosis
blocks.title: How the idea developed
blocks.body:
**Scripture.** 2 Pet 1:4 speaks of becoming "partakers of the divine nature"; Jesus cites Ps 82:6, "you are gods" (John 10:34); Paul speaks of being transformed into Christ's image from glory to glory (2 Cor 3:18).

**Fathers.** Irenaeus, Clement and Athanasius summed up the gospel in an exchange: the Son became what we are so that we might become what he is. The Cappadocians, Cyril and Maximus developed this: by union with the incarnate Son, through the Spirit, we share God's life without becoming God by nature. Pseudo-Dionysius gave the classic definition of *theosis* as likeness and union with God.

**Byzantine theology.** Symeon taught that this union can be consciously known. Gregory Palamas distinguished God's essence (unknowable) from his energies (truly shared), a teaching upheld by councils in Constantinople (1341–1351).

**West.** Augustine and Aquinas also spoke of deification and participation, though Western theology after the Reformation focused on legal categories. Wesley, the Anglicans, and recent Lutheran and Reformed scholars have rediscovered the theme.

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/theosis
blocks.title: How the relational tradition reads it
blocks.body:
Theosis is what the relational gospel is about. The Father's goal was never only to acquit us but to share his life with us as sons and daughters (Gal 4:4–7). In the Son we are adopted; by the Spirit we are drawn into the communion of Father and Son.

This is not human self-improvement or absorption into God. It is union with Christ, who remains the one Mediator, and it looks like him: humble, self-giving love (Phil 2:5–11).

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/satisfaction-theory
blocks.title: How the idea developed
blocks.body:
**Latin roots.** Tertullian and Cyprian used *satisfactio* for acts of penance by which a sinner made amends to God and the church. The medieval penitential system developed this into a system of satisfactions.

**Anselm.** In *Cur Deus Homo* Anselm rejected the idea that the devil had rights over humanity. Sin, he argued, withholds from God the honour owed to him; God's justice requires either satisfaction or punishment. Humanity owes it but cannot pay; only God can pay. So God becomes man, and Christ's freely given death, of infinite worth, restores God's honour and merits a reward that he passes to us.

**After Anselm.** Abelard emphasised the cross as the display of God's love. Aquinas refined Anselm: Christ's satisfaction flows from love and obedience and is "superabundant". Trent adopted satisfaction language. The Reformers took the further step of making satisfaction *penal*, the transfer of punishment.

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/satisfaction-theory
blocks.title: How the legal reading arose
blocks.body:
Satisfaction theory is the bridge between the patristic and the Reformation legal readings. Its frame is a feudal court of honour and the church's penitential law: wrong creates a debt that must be paid. Anselm explicitly offered satisfaction as an alternative to punishment, but by putting the cross inside a system of debts owed to God, he prepared the way for Calvin's penal version.

Relational authors note that the Fathers did not ask "what does God need?" but "what do we need?" God needed nothing; we needed healing, freedom from death, and union with him.

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/satisfaction-theory
blocks.title: How the relational tradition reads it
blocks.body:
Anselm rightly saw that only God can save and that he does it as a human being, from within. The relational reading keeps that insight and drops the bookkeeping. Christ's obedience is not a payment to the Father but the Son's lifelong "yes" to the Father as one of us, healing our "no" (Rom 5:19; Phil 2:8).

What is "satisfied" is the Father's desire to have his children home, not a debt of honour.

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/limited-atonement
blocks.title: How the idea developed
blocks.body:
**Augustine.** Augustine's strong doctrine of predestination led him to read "God desires all people to be saved" (1 Tim 2:4) as all *kinds* of people.

**Medieval debates.** The monk Gottschalk taught double predestination and that Christ died only for the elect; he was condemned at Quierzy (849/853), which affirmed that Christ suffered for all. Peter Lombard's formula, that Christ's death is sufficient for all but efficient only for the elect, became standard.

**Reformation.** Calvin's view is debated: he wrote strongly of election, but also commented on texts like 1 John 2:2 and 2 Cor 5:19 in broad terms. Beza and later Reformed orthodoxy taught that Christ died specifically for the elect. Against the Remonstrants, the Synod of Dort (1619) affirmed that Christ's death effectively redeems all and only the elect, while holding it sufficient for the whole world. John Owen's *Death of Death* (1647) gave the classic defence.

**Later.** Amyraut and the English hypothetical universalists softened it; Barth reconceived election in Christ for all. The acronym TULIP dates from the early twentieth century.

citations.ref: Second Head of Doctrine, articles 3 and 8
The Death of Death in the Death of Christ

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/limited-atonement
blocks.title: How the legal reading arose
blocks.body:
Limited atonement follows from a legal logic: if Christ paid the exact penal debt of particular persons, then those debts cannot be charged again, so he must have paid only for those who will be saved (Owen's "double payment" argument). The atonement becomes a commercial or judicial transaction with a fixed list of beneficiaries.

Relational authors (including Barth, T. F. and J. B. Torrance) answer that the atonement is first about who Christ is: the eternal Son united to all humanity in the incarnation. Christ is "the propitiation… for the sins of the whole world" (1 John 2:2).

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/limited-atonement
blocks.title: How the relational tradition reads it
blocks.body:
Jesus reveals a Father who leaves the ninety-nine to look for the one (Luke 15:4) and who "so loved the world" (John 3:16). The relational reading starts from the incarnation: the Son took on our shared humanity, so his life, death and resurrection concern every human being (2 Cor 5:14–15).

That does not erase human response. Love can be refused. But no one stands outside the Father's love or Christ's self-offering. The question is not whether God has included us, but whether we will receive it.

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/purgatory
blocks.title: How the idea developed
blocks.body:
**Prayer for the dead.** 2 Maccabees 12:43–45 describes an offering for dead soldiers. Early Christians prayed and offered the Eucharist for the departed: Tertullian mentions offerings on anniversaries, and the *Passion of Perpetua* records her prayers for her brother.

**Purification.** Clement and Origen spoke of fire that purifies after death. Augustine allowed that some may be purified through fire before the final judgement, reading 1 Cor 3:15. Gregory the Great's *Dialogues* spoke of a purging fire for lesser faults and told stories of souls helped by Masses.

**Medieval doctrine.** In the twelfth century "purgatory" became a noun for a place. Lyon II (1274) and Florence (1439) defined it; the Orthodox accepted prayer for the dead but rejected juridical satisfaction and a purgatorial fire. The sale of indulgences for souls in purgatory provoked Luther's theses (1517). Trent affirmed purgatory (1563); Protestant confessions rejected it.

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/purgatory
blocks.title: How the legal reading arose
blocks.body:
The Latin form of purgatory rests on a legal distinction: forgiveness removes the eternal guilt of sin, but a "temporal punishment" remains owed and must be paid (satisfaction), either in this life or after death. Indulgences drew on a "treasury of merits" to remit that debt. This is the penitential, satisfaction framework applied beyond death.

The Eastern Orthodox and relational authors keep the idea of growth and healing after death but reject the idea of outstanding penalties to be paid.

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/purgatory
blocks.title: How the relational tradition reads it
blocks.body:
The relational reading asks what God's fire is for. The Father's purpose is to heal and perfect his children (Heb 12:10). If there is transformation after death, it is the work of love, not the payment of a debt. Christ's work is complete and no further penalty is owed (Rom 8:1).

Many Christians, Protestant and Orthodox, can affirm that we will be made fully like Christ when we see him (1 John 3:2), and that this involves facing the truth about ourselves in the light of his love (1 Cor 3:13–15).

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/sola-scriptura
blocks.title: How the idea developed
blocks.body:
**Early church.** The Fathers treated Scripture as the supreme authority, read within the apostolic "rule of faith" handed down in the churches. Irenaeus appealed to both against the Gnostics. Athanasius called the Scriptures sufficient for declaring the truth; Cyril of Jerusalem told catechumens not to believe even him without proof from Scripture.

**Medieval and Reformation.** As church authority grew, critics such as Wycliffe and Hus appealed to Scripture against popes and councils. Luther at Worms (1521) refused to recant unless convinced by Scripture and plain reason. The Reformers did not reject tradition (they kept the creeds and read the Fathers) but held that Scripture alone is the final, infallible norm (*norma normans*).

**Responses.** Trent (1546) taught that revelation is contained in Scripture and unwritten traditions. Vatican II's *Dei Verbum* spoke of Scripture and Tradition flowing from one divine source. Radical and restorationist movements later turned *sola scriptura* into "no creed but the Bible" (sometimes called *solo scriptura*).

blocks.subject: entry:doctrine/sola-scriptura
blocks.title: How the relational tradition reads it
blocks.body:
The relational tradition honours Scripture as the Spirit-breathed witness to Christ (2 Tim 3:16). But Jesus himself is the Word; the Scriptures testify about him (John 5:39–40). So we read the whole Bible through Jesus, who is perfect theology.

Read this way, the question is not only "Scripture or tradition?" but "Christ-centred reading or not?" The Fathers' rule of faith was a Christ-shaped way of reading, and it is a help, not a rival, to Scripture.
